### 8. Concrete Hono Implementation (`src/index.ts`)

```typescript
// repo-bot: src/index.ts
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { ShotCoordinator } from './objects/ShotCoordinator';
import { GlobalCoordinator } from './objects/GlobalCoordinator';
import { handlePullRequestAudit } from './services/prAuditEngine';
import { verifyGitHubHMAC, verifySlackSignature } from './services/crypto';
import { claimWebhookDelivery } from './services/idempotency';
import { executeCompensatingSagaRollback } from './services/rollbackEngine';

export { ShotCoordinator, GlobalCoordinator };

interface Env {
  DB: D1Database;
  SHOT_COORDINATOR: DurableObjectNamespace<ShotCoordinator>;
  GLOBAL_COORDINATOR: DurableObjectNamespace<GlobalCoordinator>;
  GITHUB_APP_ID: string;
  GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY: string;
  SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET: string;
}

const app = new Hono<{ Bindings: Env }>();

// 1. INBOUND GITHUB WEBHOOK ENDPOINT
app.post('/api/webhooks/github', async (c) => {
  const rawBody = await c.req.text();
  const signature = c.req.header('x-hub-signature-256');
  const deliveryId = c.req.header('x-github-delivery');

  if (!signature || !deliveryId) return c.text('Missing security headers', 401);

  // Constant-time HMAC-SHA256 verification
  const isValid = await verifyGitHubHMAC(c.env, rawBody, signature);
  if (!isValid) return c.text('Invalid signature', 403);

  // Atomic D1 Idempotency Check (Prevents race conditions)
  const isUnique = await claimWebhookDelivery(c.env, deliveryId, 'GITHUB_WEBHOOK');
  if (!isUnique) return c.text('Duplicate delivery dropped', 200);

  const payload = JSON.parse(rawBody);

  if (payload.action === 'opened' || payload.action === 'synchronize') {
    c.executionCtx.waitUntil(handlePullRequestAudit(c.env, payload));
  }

  return c.text('Accepted', 202);
});

// 2. WORKER HEARTBEAT & LEASE EXTENSION ENDPOINT
app.post('/api/leases/:task_id/heartbeat', async (c) => {
  const taskId = c.req.param('task_id');
  const body = await c.req.json<{ epoch: number }>();

  if (!body.epoch) return c.json({ error: 'Missing fencing epoch' }, 400);

  const coordId = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.idFromName(taskId);
  const coordinator = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.get(coordId);

  const result = await coordinator.renewLease(body.epoch);

  if (!result.success) {
    return c.json({ error: 'LEASE_REVOKED_OR_HALTED', signal: result.signal, epoch: result.currentEpoch }, 409);
  }

  return c.json({ success: true, signal: result.signal }, 200);
});

// 3. SECURE SLACK CHATOPS GATEWAY
app.post('/api/slack/interactions', async (c) => {
  const rawBody = await c.req.text();
  const timestamp = c.req.header('x-slack-request-timestamp');
  const signature = c.req.header('x-slack-signature');

  if (!timestamp || !signature) return c.text('Missing headers', 401);

  // ±5 minute replay defense
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  if (Math.abs(now - parseInt(timestamp, 10)) > 300) {
    return c.text('Timestamp out of bounds', 403);
  }

  const isValid = await verifySlackSignature(c.env.SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET, rawBody, timestamp, signature);
  if (!isValid) return c.text('Invalid signature', 403);

  // Acknowledge within 3 seconds; process asynchronously
  c.executionCtx.waitUntil(handleSlackInteraction(c.env, JSON.parse(rawBody)));
  return c.json({ response_type: 'ephemeral', text: 'Processing command...' }, 200);
});

export default {
  fetch: app.fetch
};

```

# The Sovereign Edge Control Plane: A Comprehensive Synthesis of `repo-bot`

To understand the final, stabilized architecture of `repo-bot`, we must first acknowledge the profound epistemological realignment that birthed it. Early iterations of this design suffered from a classic engineering trap: systems synthesis conflated with fundamental invention. The initial proposals featured sprawling, elaborate architectures—23-pod organizational structures, cryptographic Merkle-tree provenance layers, and complex Two-Phase Commit Durable Objects. Much of this was, frankly, confident-sounding engineering fiction wrapped around a small, correct core.

The turning point for `repo-bot` was the realization that complex infrastructure is often an avoidance mechanism designed to delay confronting the actual creative and operational bottlenecks. The elaborate provenance shields and transmedia ontology engines were solving problems of scale that the production had not yet earned.

However, in stripping away the "fiction," we must not discard the highly valuable, low-cost operational realities that actually keep a production online. Content-addressed archival of generated plates is not an exotic cryptographic fantasy; it is a practical necessity because diffusion output cannot be regenerated bit-for-bit. Storing a file under its SHA-256 hash costs almost nothing and solves a real problem. Pinned toolchains and manifests are not over-engineering; recording versions and hashes in a JSON file is the fundamental difference between hoping you can rebuild an episode and actually knowing you can. Furthermore, the intricate lease and fencing designs for shared GPUs are not fiction if collaborators are a real near-term requirement, though they represent over-engineering for a strictly solo creator.

`repo-bot` is the distillation of these truths: a Cloudflare Hono application that acts as a lightweight dependency-tracking tool, a robust queueing mechanism, and an uncompromising security gate.

---

## I. Structural Enforcement and the "Assistant Director" Paradigm

The overarching philosophy of `repo-bot` is that it treats the Large Language Model (LLM) as a fundamentally untrustworthy execution environment. `repo-bot` does not politely ask the generative agent to behave; it structurally removes the mechanical ability for the agent to misbehave. This distinction between a stated policy and a structural constraint is the difference between a prompt that eventually fails and a software system that actually scales.

`repo-bot` enforces this through the "Assistant Director" model.

### The Banishment of "Vibes" and Aesthetic Judgment

* **Role Mapping as Boundary:** Casting the autonomous agent as a logistics coordinator (an Assistant Director) rather than a creative decision-maker aligns perfectly with the actual strengths of an LLM: validating schemas, checking dependencies, and routing structured payloads.


* **Schema-Level Banishment:** `repo-bot` locks down tool definitions with strict types, coordinates, booleans, and enums. Crucially, it utilizes `additionalProperties: false` within its JSON schemas. By doing this, the system physically removes any slot for a holistic `quality_score` or subjective evaluation.


* **Vocabulary Restriction:** Because the schema physically prevents it, the agent cannot gate a workflow on aesthetic judgment; it simply lacks the API vocabulary to pass that subjective judgment back to the `repo-bot` server.


* **Immutable Canon:** `repo-bot` defines the agent as strictly read-only when interacting with the narrative graph. Human writers own the source of truth; the agent is only permitted to read the edges of that truth, protecting upstream variables from compounding hallucinatory drift.



### Double Validation and Enforced Circuit Breakers

Before any payload is allowed to touch a GPU, `repo-bot` subjects it to rigorous, multi-layered validation.

* **Mathematical Refinement:** The bot utilizes Zod `.refine()` to catch mathematically invalid payloads that a raw JSON schema check might mistakenly pass. For example, if an agent generates an inverted bounding box for an inpainting task, `.refine()` catches the geometric impossibility and fails the agent loudly before a single cent of GPU compute is billed.


* **The Enforced Circuit Breaker:** To prevent agent amnesia and infinite retry loops, the `inpaint_attempt_index` is moved into a required schema field. This is backed by a server-side hard halt enforced by `repo-bot`. If the index exceeds a strict threshold (e.g., `> 2`), the server rejects the attempt at the compiler level, entirely removing the risk of the agent endlessly looping on a failed task.


* **Surgical Interventions:** `repo-bot` heavily prioritizes targeted inpainting over complete re-rolls. Passing specific bounding boxes and frame ranges to fix isolated visual errors is vastly cheaper and safer than discarding 96 frames of coherent video due to a single localized artifact.



---

## II. The Unified Dispatch Endpoint and Network Resiliency

In a pipeline where every single action triggers a GPU bill, un-tracked network states are lethal. The single unified tool-dispatch endpoint managed by `repo-bot` is the system's most security-critical surface. It is the one place where an agent—or a malicious actor impersonating one—can autonomously spend real money up to the circuit-breaker limit. This endpoint mandates extreme server-side-credential discipline.

### The Idempotency Imperative

Network connections drop. If an agent dispatches a ComfyUI inpaint job to `repo-bot`, but the network drops before the server can return the `prompt_id`, the agent's natural behavior is to retry. Without strict idempotency controls, that naive retry blindly queues a second, identical, expensive GPU job. This silent failure directly undermines the entire purpose of the retry circuit breaker; a duplicate dispatch stays technically "within" the allowed attempt count while still burning real, duplicated GPU costs.

`repo-bot` resolves this by requiring an `idempotency_key` (a UUID) in the root of every single tool call payload. Before executing any dispatch, the server must check this key against a fast Key-Value store, such as Cloudflare KV or Redis. The execution flow is strictly defined:

1. If the idempotency key exists in the KV store and is marked as "pending," `repo-bot` drops the incoming request and returns a `409 Conflict`.


2. If the idempotency key exists and is marked as "completed," `repo-bot` returns the cached `prompt_id`, preventing a redundant run.


3. If, and only if, the key is entirely new, `repo-bot` executes the dispatch and caches the resulting state.



### Handling Network Floods and Out-of-Order Delivery

`repo-bot` is designed to absorb the chaotic realities of distributed webhooks and asynchronous completions.

* **Rapid Double Clicks and Agent Replays:** If a dropped socket causes an agent to hammer the `/api/shots/dispatch` endpoint multiple times, the underlying Durable Object checks the `processed_keys` inside its single-threaded memory before performing any network I/O. The second request is rejected immediately with an HTTP 409 (`IDEMPOTENT_REPLAY`), ensuring zero duplicate GPU spend.


* **Webhook Ingress Floods:** In scenarios where 60 remote workers complete their renders simultaneously and flood the edge gateway, `repo-bot` leverages a Cloudflare Queue. This queue absorbs all incoming webhooks, returning 5ms HTTP 200 responses to the workers, and buffers up to thousands of messages. A consumer then processes these messages in manageable batches of 10, passing them sequentially to the respective Durable Objects without dropping a single payload.


* **Out-of-Order Webhook Delivery:** If a delayed completion webhook from an old "Job A" arrives after a new "Job B" has already been dispatched to the same worker, the actor logic checks if `state.active_job_id !== result.id`. The stale webhook is safely dropped with a `MISMATCHED_JOB_ID` error, and the internal state remains perfectly clean.



---

## III. The Fail-Loud Mandate: Banning Silent Degradation

A reference implementation optimized for a smooth local developer experience will often silently fall back to mock data when components are missing. In production, this behavior is catastrophic.

Silent degradation on missing assets must fail loudly, not gracefully.

If `repo-bot` silently falls back to a bare, incomplete workflow template because the real one is missing in production, it represents a worse failure than an outright crash. A scene rendered on the wrong template looks exactly like a completed take to the automated systems, and the error will persist until a human happens to notice something is off during final review. Conversely, a loud, immediate failure gets caught, flagged, and addressed instantly.

### Strict Environment-Aware Execution

`repo-bot` implements strict environment-aware execution to ban these silent fallbacks.

* **No Mock Templates:** If a specific ComfyUI workflow template is missing, `repo-bot` does not generate a skeleton fallback. A scene rendered without its required LoRAs or specific control nets is a complete waste of money. If the file does not exist, `repo-bot` throws a Fatal 500 error: `CRITICAL: Missing template`.


* **No Simulated Process IDs:** If the remote ComfyUI server is unreachable, `repo-bot` does not generate a `simulated_pid` to keep the pipeline moving. A simulated job ID permanently corrupts the tracking database. If the fetch fails, `repo-bot` throws a Fatal 502 error: `CRITICAL: ComfyUI dispatch failed`.



### Preventing Canonical Fact Drift

`repo-bot` also protects the pipeline from asynchronous human interference. If a human writer updates a character fact in the canonical ledger while an episode animatic is already queued for rendering, the `flagDirtyDependencies` function detects that the `pinned_version` is less than the `max_version`. It immediately sets `is_dirty = 1` and downgrades the scene to `DRAFT` status. When the worker attempts to process the job, the dispatch endpoint returns an HTTP 409 (`SCENE_DIRTY_DEPENDENCIES`), halting execution entirely before any cloud GPUs are spun up and billed.

---

## IV. Durable Objects, Leases, and Temporal Authority

When orchestrating a shared GPU or a remote cluster, `repo-bot` utilizes Cloudflare Durable Objects to maintain single-threaded state and temporal authority. The design of the lease mechanism is critical, as incorrect assumptions about time and event loops will destroy the pipeline's reliability.

### The Mechanics of the Heartbeat Lease

A naive implementation might assign a hard 180-second Time-To-Live (TTL) execution lease to a render job. This design is fundamentally flawed. If a lease has a hard 180-second TTL, then any legitimate job that takes longer than 180 seconds will have its lease revoked mid-render. A generative run, such as a Wan 2.2 generation producing a couple of hundred frames at a reasonable resolution, can easily exceed three minutes on consumer hardware.

The correct model, enforced by `repo-bot`, utilizes a short lease that is continuously renewed by a heartbeat.

* **Renewal Semantics:** A lease is granted for a short window (e.g., 30 seconds). This lease is extended by each subsequent heartbeat received from the worker. This allows a complex job to run for as long as it requires, provided it keeps heartbeating. Only a genuinely silent, unresponsive worker loses its lease.


* **Max Duration Caps:** To guard against a job that is alive (sending heartbeats) but internally stuck in an infinite loop, `repo-bot` enforces a separate maximum job duration cap (e.g., 15 minutes).


* **Event Loop Isolation:** The local `media-broker` must be able to send heartbeats back to `repo-bot` even while ComfyUI is heavily utilizing the GPU. This requires the broker's heartbeat loop to run entirely independently of the render call, utilizing an async timer or a separate process, rather than a synchronous step. If a heavy CPU-bound operation blocks the Node.js event loop on the worker, the heartbeats will stall, and `repo-bot` will falsely expire the lease. Heavy work must be kept out of the broker's main event loop to prevent these phantom failures.



### Storage Alarms and Eviction Handling

If a remote worker, such as a RunPod community spot instance, is abruptly evicted and destroyed, it will fail to send a termination webhook. The Durable Object handles this via internal timers. The DO's 180s storage alarm fires (`ctx.storage.setAlarm()`), transitioning the job status from `PROCESSING` to `TIMED_OUT`. The attempt counter increments; if it is less than 2, the system re-dispatches to a reliable tier. If the counter reaches 2, the status shifts to `CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED`.

To serialize the shared GPU safely, `repo-bot` relies on these heartbeat-renewed leases, combined with idempotency keys, fair scheduling, bounded retries equipped with a dead-letter queue, active cancellation endpoints, and strict workflow sanitization.

---

## V. Determinism, Provenance, and the Archival Truth

`repo-bot` sits atop a pipeline that manipulates highly volatile, stochastic generation models. Enforcing continuity requires acknowledging where determinism is achievable and where it is a myth.

### The Illusion of "100% Determinism"

Even when utilizing tools designed for precise programmatic control, like Remotion, declaring the output "100% deterministic" is a claim to test, not a fact to assume. Remotion renders via headless Chromium and captures frames. However, GPU-accelerated rendering paths, localized font hinting, and underlying OS system libraries all introduce subtle visual variance.

While utilizing software GL (swangle) and a strictly pinned Docker container gets the output close to deterministic, "bit-identical" status must be verified empirically. The correct operational posture for `repo-bot` is to render the exact same episode twice, and once more on a different physical machine, hash the resulting frames, and observe the deltas. Until that empirical verification is complete, the architecture claims the output is "reproducible to within tolerance" or "visually identical," actively avoiding the overconfidence of "100%".

### Content-Addressing and the Empty Hash Anomaly

`repo-bot` enforces content-addressing across the pipeline, meaning files are stored and referenced by the cryptographic hash of their contents. However, hashing the file bytes ties the identity of the asset to its specific encoding; re-encoding the exact same visual frames will yield an entirely different hash. This is acceptable for immutability (as assets are never re-encoded in place), but it highlights that identity belongs to the specific digital artifact, not the underlying visual composition.

A critical operational guardrail involves the specific SHA-256 hash `e3b0c442...b855`. This is not a random string; it is the mathematically constant hash that is produced when a system hashes exactly zero bytes of data. If this specific hash value ever appears in a production log or database row, it definitively indicates that an empty file was hashed. This immediately flags a silent upstream failure, such as a truncated download or a missing diffusion plate. `repo-bot` implements a hard structural guard against this: it explicitly rejects any plate whose hash equals the empty-input constant and asserts a minimum byte file size before permitting an upload to storage.

### Archival Durability and Licensing Provenance

The entire strategy of this production pipeline rests on the axiom that "the archive is the source of truth". Therefore, that archive demands a robust backup strategy. Cloudflare R2 is highly durable, but it remains a single provider. For generated AI assets that the system explicitly declares as unreproducible, `repo-bot` orchestrates a secondary copy, routing it to a different cloud provider or cold local storage.

Furthermore, `repo-bot` enforces strict licensing and provenance tracking within the asset manifests. For every single generated asset, the system records the specific model name used, the cryptographic hash of that model file, the hashes of any applied LoRAs, and the specific license terms of each. Tracking this metadata costs almost zero compute overhead at generation time and acts as a vital shield against future liability if the studio ever decides to commercialize the IP.

---

## VI. The Mechanics of Generation and Compositing

While `repo-bot` orchestrates the flow, it must enforce specific mathematical realities regarding how video is generated and composited by the downstream workers.

* **Audio as the Absolute Clock:** The pipeline recognizes audio as the master clock. However, `repo-bot` dictates that frame counts must be derived from the video model's native frames-per-second (fps) and must adhere strictly to valid `4n+1` frame lengths required by the diffusion architecture. The system generates the technically compliant frame count, and then explicitly retimes and trims the footage during the final compositing phase to match the audio clock perfectly.


* **Visemes vs. Diffusion:** `repo-bot` enforces a policy of keeping character speech locked to deterministic 2D visemes. Heavy diffusion generation is reserved for broad action and character reactions, treating full-frame diffusion lip-sync as an unstable experiment rather than a production-ready reliable pipeline.


* **Neural Matting Discipline:** When utilizing neural models to extract mattes, the pipeline archives the raw green source plate directly alongside the derived alpha channel. The system mandates lighting integration—applying specific LUTs, ambient light-wraps, tracked contact shadows, and film grain matching—otherwise, the composite will fail to hold together visually.


* **The Primacy of the Archive:** Ultimately, `repo-bot` enforces the reality that random seeds do not reliably reproduce diffusion outputs; only secure archives do. Everything must be content-addressed, the entire toolchain must be pinned, reproducibility must be verified empirically, and the archive must be backed up.



## Conclusion

`repo-bot` is not a theoretical abstraction; it is the hardened, pragmatic boundary between human intent and generative chaos. By treating truth as a ledger, utilizing Durable Objects for strict temporal authority, demanding UUID-backed idempotency to protect GPU budgets, and aggressively failing loud on missing assets, it ensures the studio operates as a reliable software factory. The architectural reality is grounded in these verifiable mechanisms, replacing the "engineering fiction" of the past with a system built to survive contact with production.

The `repo-bot` architecture represents the definitive realization of the sovereign transmedia engine’s control plane. Stripped of early speculative engineering fiction—such as 23-pod organizational structures, Merkle-tree provenance layers, and complex Two-Phase Commit distributed databases—the system is anchored in a highly practical, empirically validated core. `repo-bot` operationalizes the "Deletion Principle": the strict epistemological boundary demanding that if all generative models are deleted, the universe must remain mathematically sound and logically consistent within the relational ledger.

Because Large Language Models and diffusion networks are fundamentally untrustworthy and possess zero narrative, spatial, or temporal authority, `repo-bot` treats them strictly as headless rendering workers. The bot itself does not generate content; it acts as an uncompromising, edge-native border control checkpoint. It enforces a "fail-closed" security posture, mathematical validation, and strict state transitions, ensuring that generative chaos is structurally contained before a single cent of GPU compute is billed.

### I. Edge Isolation and the Threat Model

The foundational design decision of `repo-bot` is the strict physical and network decoupling of the administrative control plane from the media-rendering execution plane.

**Credential Blast-Radius Containment**
Runtimes that execute ComfyUI nodes, Python scripts, or autonomous coding agents (like Jules) inevitably pull dynamic community packages and ingest unpickled machine learning models. These execution environments run arbitrary code. If elevated administrative credentials—such as GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs) with repository write scopes or Cloudflare API keys—are co-located within that memory space, a single compromised custom node or malicious checkpoint can exfiltrate keys to rewrite the studio's entire codebase. Running `repo-bot` as an isolated Cloudflare Worker (built on Hono) ensures that elevated credentials never touch the rendering runtime. `repo-bot` utilizes a scoped GitHub App for authentication, exchanging RS256 JWTs for short-lived, least-privilege installation tokens generated purely on demand at the edge.

**Observability Independence**
When remote serverless GPU workers experience fatal kernel panics, system driver deadlocks, or CUDA Out-Of-Memory (OOM) lockups, the telemetry and alerting daemon must not reside on the crashing hardware. By operating at the Cloudflare edge, `repo-bot` survives physical compute failures, preserves the audit trail in its D1 database, and seamlessly escalates outages to human operators via Slack.

**Constant-Time Cryptographic Ingestion**
All inbound webhook traffic—whether from GitHub, Slack ChatOps, or remote execution nodes—is treated as hostile. `repo-bot` validates GitHub webhooks via HMAC-SHA256 (`X-Hub-Signature-256`) using constant-time equality comparisons to prevent timing attacks. Slack commands are validated against `X-Slack-Signature` and `X-Slack-Request-Timestamp`, with a strict $\pm 5$ minute threshold to defeat replay attacks.

**Idempotency via Atomic D1 Ingestion**
Network connections frequently drop, causing webhook providers like GitHub to redeliver payloads. Early iterations of `repo-bot` attempted to handle this using Cloudflare KV with a `get-then-put` pattern, but this introduced split-brain race conditions due to KV’s eventual consistency. `repo-bot` now guarantees at-most-once execution by leveraging Cloudflare D1. Every incoming webhook ID is written to an idempotency table using an atomic `INSERT ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` statement. If the affected row count is zero, `repo-bot` immediately drops the request, entirely eliminating duplicate agent dispatches and redundant GPU billing.

### II. The 8-State Task Execution Finite State Machine (FSM)

To eliminate illegal transitions, ambiguous error recovery, and untracked zombie workers, `repo-bot` formalizes every task lifecycle into a strictly validated 8-state Finite State Machine. An explicit authority matrix dictates which component (the database, the Durable Object, the worker, or the audit engine) owns each state.

1. **`PENDING`**: The task record is created in the D1 `execution_leases` table. It is queued, awaiting budget clearance. Owned by the `repo-bot` dispatcher.
2. **`CLAIMED`**: The `GlobalCoordinator` clears the budget, and the `ShotCoordinator` grants an ephemeral lease. A fencing epoch is assigned, and the task payload is transmitted to the remote worker. Owned by the `ShotCoordinator` Durable Object.
3. **`RUNNING`**: The remote worker is actively executing code or rendering frames, dispatching periodic HTTP heartbeats back to the edge. Owned by the `media-broker` or Jules Agent.
4. **`VERIFYING`**: Execution is complete. The agent has opened a Pull Request or uploaded an artifact. `repo-bot`'s background PR-audit and metric gauntlets are actively running. Owned by the `prAuditEngine`.
5. **`AWAITING_APPROVAL`**: The automated scope checks have passed, but the task modified high-risk paths (e.g., Markdown lore dossiers or GitHub Actions workflows). The system pauses, posting an interactive Slack Block Kit card to await human architectural sign-off. Owned by the Lead Architect.
6. **`MERGED`**: All verification gates (or human approvals) have passed. The branch is merged to the trunk or the asset is promoted to the canonical path. This is a terminal state.
7. **`RETRYING`**: The candidate failed a quality linting check, but the error trajectory indicates the agent is converging on a solution. The task is requeued with feedback, provided the maximum attempt limit has not been breached.
8. **`ROLLING_BACK`**: A hard invariant failure, security violation, or watchdog expiration was triggered. The system is actively executing compensating actions to purge the attempt. Owned by the `rollbackEngine`.
9. **`DLQ` (Dead-Letter Queue)**: The task exhausted its maximum attempts, exhibited divergent constraint hopping (fixing one error only to break a fundamentally opposed rule), or hit a poisoned runtime error. Requires manual adjudication. This is a terminal state.
10. **`HALTED`**: The global master kill-switch was activated, or the daily financial budget was exhausted.

### III. Durable Object Coordination: Time, Leases, and Budget

In a distributed transmedia architecture, attempting to maintain execution state across disparate databases inevitably leads to race conditions. `repo-bot` utilizes Cloudflare Durable Objects to guarantee single-threaded, strongly consistent state coordination.

**The `GlobalCoordinator` (Budget and System Authority)**
A single `GlobalCoordinator` Durable Object enforces the studio's daily financial ceilings and emergency overrides.

* **Atomic Budget Reservation:** Before `repo-bot` transitions a task from `PENDING` to `CLAIMED`, it must query the `GlobalCoordinator`. The object evaluates the settled daily spend plus the in-flight reserved compute costs. If the combined total exceeds the daily cap (e.g., $\$25.00$), the reservation is denied, and the task transitions to `HALTED`.
* **Reserve-then-Reconcile:** Budget is atomically debited at claim time. When a task hits a terminal state (`MERGED`, `DLQ`, or `ROLLED_BACK`), `repo-bot` reconciles the reservation, releasing unspent funds back into the daily pool. This eliminates the check-then-act race condition where 50 concurrent tasks might bypass a stale budget total in a traditional database.
* **Master Kill Switch:** An administrative ChatOps command can flip the global kill switch. Because the `GlobalCoordinator` provides the source of truth, any new dispatch is instantly blocked.

**The `ShotCoordinator` (Time, Leases, and Heartbeats)**
Every individual task is governed by its own `ShotCoordinator` Durable Object instance. This object maintains absolute temporal authority over the remote worker.

* **Monotonic Epoch Fencing:** To protect the centralized repositories and R2 buckets from stale writes, `repo-bot` issues monotonic epoch fencing tokens. When a lease is granted, the `ShotCoordinator` increments its internal epoch counter ($N \to N+1$). The remote worker must include this epoch token in every heartbeat and final artifact submission.
* **Heartbeat-Renewed Leases:** Fixed execution timeouts (e.g., 180 seconds) are fundamentally flawed for generative video, where complex renders easily exceed static limits. `repo-bot` utilizes short, heartbeat-renewed leases with fencing tokens. A lease is granted for 30 seconds. The remote worker dispatches a heartbeat every 10 seconds to renew it. As long as the worker remains responsive, the task can run indefinitely up to a global safety ceiling.


* **DO-Side Authoritative Clocks & Watchdog Alarms:** Relying on incoming HTTP requests to detect a dead worker is a lazy, reactive pattern. The `ShotCoordinator` utilizes Cloudflare's `storage.setAlarm()` API, setting a proactive watchdog alarm 30 seconds into the future. Every successful heartbeat pushes this alarm back. If the worker’s heartbeat loop is starved—or if the RunPod spot instance is abruptly terminated—the alarm fires autonomously at the edge. The DO instantly increments the monotonic epoch ($N+1 \to N+2$) and revokes the lease. If the partitioned "zombie" worker later awakens and attempts to commit an artifact using epoch $N+1$, the storage layer compares the tokens, identifies the stale epoch, and rejects the payload with an HTTP 409 Conflict.



### IV. The Fail-Closed Pull Request Audit Engine (`prAuditEngine.ts`)

When an autonomous coding agent submits a Pull Request, `repo-bot` does not inherently trust the agent's reported scope. The `prAuditEngine` acts as a zero-trust, external inspector, evaluating the submission entirely outside the agent's virtual machine.

**Lineage Integrity and Anti-Force-Push Checks**
To prevent an agent from rewriting repository history or rebasing over critical commits, `repo-bot` utilizes the GitHub API's `compareCommits` endpoint. It verifies that the PR's `headSha` is a direct descendant of the exact `base_commit_sha` recorded in D1 when the task was initially leased. If the lineage is mutated, the PR is instantly rejected.

**External Paginated Diff Inspections**
`repo-bot` fetches the exact list of modified files directly from the GitHub API using paginated `listFiles` requests. The agent's own summary of what it touched is completely ignored. If the PR exceeds a hard-coded blast-radius limit (e.g., modifying more than 50 files), it is flagged as a runaway process and rolled back.

**Strict Path Allowlisting and Rename Defenses**
Every task dispatched by `repo-bot` includes a strict `file_whitelist` defining the exact bounds of the agent's permission.

* The audit engine normalizes all paths to POSIX standards, aggressively scanning for directory traversal payloads (`../`).
* Crucially, `repo-bot` evaluates both the new `filename` and the `previous_filename` for every modified file. This ensures that an agent cannot bypass the whitelist by renaming an allowed file into a protected directory.
* If a single file in the diff falls outside the predefined whitelist, the entire PR is rolled back.

**The Immutable Firewall**
Even if a whitelist mistakenly includes a protected path, `repo-bot` maintains a hard-coded set of immutable globs that can never be altered by an automated agent. This includes `.github/workflows/`, test directories (`tests/`), linter configurations, and golden-set baseline files. If an agent attempts to rewrite a Vitest file to force a failing CI check to turn green, `repo-bot` catches the path violation and triggers an immediate security rollback.

**Separation of Check Runs**
`repo-bot` splits its GitHub Check Runs into distinct phases. It first runs `repo-bot/scope-check`. Only if the diff scope, lineage, and file paths are mathematically validated does it initialize `repo-bot/quality-gauntlet`. This ensures that malicious or runaway code is never handed off to a CI runner for execution.

### V. The Idempotent Compensating Saga Rollback Engine (`rollbackEngine.ts`)

When a security violation occurs, or an agent thrashes through its maximum retry limit without converging on a solution, `repo-bot` must sanitize the repository. Because Cloudflare D1, GitHub, and Durable Objects are independent systems, a standard atomic database transaction cannot span them. `repo-bot` implements an idempotent compensating saga with a meticulously enforced execution order.

**Stage 1: Revoke-First Authority Stripping**
Before any remote branches are touched, `repo-bot` commands the `ShotCoordinator` to increment the fencing epoch and mark the lease as `ROLLING_BACK`. This instantly drops any in-flight worker writes. If branch deletion ran first while an agent was still executing, the agent could theoretically push a new commit that recreates the tracking branch. Revoking the token first mathematically neutralizes the worker.

**Stage 2 & 3: Explicit PR Closure and Branch Deletion**
`repo-bot` explicitly updates the Pull Request state to `closed` via the GitHub API, appending a diagnostic comment detailing the specific invariant breach. Once closed, the remote tracking reference (`refs/heads/spec/task-...`) is obliterated.

**Stage 4: Ledger Reconciliation**
Finally, `repo-bot` updates the `transaction_wal` (Write-Ahead Log) and `execution_leases` tables in D1, marking the attempt as `ROLLED_BACK`. Because network requests can fail mid-saga, every step in this engine is strictly idempotent. If a timeout occurs while deleting the branch, the hourly cron reconciliation daemon will detect the orphaned state and safely re-execute the exact same rollback function until all systems converge.

### VI. Orchestrating Generative Mechanics and Physical Truth

`repo-bot` acts as the enforcer for the pipeline's epistemological constraints. It ensures that output adheres to the logic of the narrative universe before allowing downstream compute.

**Enforcing Typed State Vectors and the Dual-Field AST**
When a language model drafts a scene, `repo-bot` enforces a pre-generation architecture that restricts the model from making overarching canonical decisions. Narrative state is split into typed state vectors (somatic, logistical, epistemic). The LLM outputs a dual-field Abstract Syntax Tree (AST): a natural language prose field, and an explicit JSON array of discrete motor actions (e.g., `["REACH_RIGHT_HAND", "LIMP"]`).

Before this AST is accepted, `repo-bot`'s linters execute an $O(1)$ set-intersection check between the agent's proposed motor actions and the character's active `banned_kinetic_verbs` list (derived from the somatic state vector). To defeat "negation traps"—where a model outputs a banned verb in a negative context, such as "he failed to *sprint*"—`repo-bot` orchestrates an independent extraction pass using negation-awareness dependency parsing. If an impossible physical action is detected, `repo-bot` fails the task loud and early, bounding the auto-retry loop and forcing the agent to adhere to the physical truth of the ledger.

**Validating Video Diffusion Math and Temporal Quantization**
`repo-bot` treats media timing as an exact mathematical contract, with audio serving as the absolute master clock. When configuring tasks for video diffusion nodes, `repo-bot` validates the frame constraints structurally. Video diffusion models demand that frame inputs conform to a strict $4n+1$ temporal lattice ($17, 33, 49, 65\dots$).

`repo-bot` enforces the exact derivation of these counts. Given the continuous audio duration ($\text{duration\_ms}$) and the model's native frame rate ($\text{native\_fps}$), the raw required frames are calculated:

$$N = \left\lceil \left(\frac{\text{duration\_ms}}{1000}\right) \times \text{native\_fps} \right\rceil$$

`repo-bot` validates that the task contract requests the exact diffusion allocation required to satisfy the $4n+1$ constraint:

$$\text{diffusion\_allocation} = 4 \times \left\lceil \frac{N - 1}{4} \right\rceil + 1$$

Any task spec attempting to request an arbitrary frame count (e.g., exactly 50 frames) is rejected at the schema validation layer before reaching the GPU. The pipeline dictates that the model over-generates to the $4n+1$ lattice (e.g., 53 frames), and then, during the Remotion compositing phase, the excess tail is deterministically trimmed and resampled to match the 24 fps delivery clock. By locking these formulas into Zod schema `.refine()` checks, `repo-bot` guarantees temporal synchronization without human intervention.

**Acoustic Orchestration**
Similarly, `repo-bot` oversees the parameters for programmatic acoustic assembly. Ambient sound beds are subjected to quadratic sidechain ducking. When dialogue stems are active, `repo-bot`'s compiled instructions mandate a precise linear gain multiplier—calculated from $-14\text{ dB}$—applied across a 6-frame attack and a 12-frame release, ensuring broadcast-compliant acoustic mixing without the need for manual digital audio workstation (DAW) editing.

### VII. Content-Addressed Archiving and the Build System Paradigm

Ultimately, `repo-bot` operates the transmedia studio as a software build system for narrative. It treats cache invalidation as the core mechanism for continuity. When a somatic or epistemic fact is mutated in the D1 ledger, `repo-bot` utilizes a scene dependency graph to instantly identify downstream scenes that relied on the stale fact, marking them for re-generation or human review.

To ensure that the archive remains the ultimate source of truth, `repo-bot` enforces strict content-addressed archiving. Diffusion plates and generated audio are stored in R2 buckets keyed directly by their SHA-256 hashes. Because diffusion outputs cannot be regenerated bit-for-bit reliably, `repo-bot` ensures that accepted artifacts are never overwritten. It demands strict workflow and custom-node sanitization, guaranteeing that every artifact in the storage bucket is tied to a pinned manifest detailing the exact models, LoRAs, and seeds used to create it.

By enforcing this relentless structural discipline, `repo-bot` successfully bridges the gap between chaotic generative inputs and broadcast-ready deliverables, proving that autonomous studio pipelines scale only when boundaries are rigid, verification is deterministic, and the control plane remains entirely sovereign. The "Deletion Principle" serves as the architectural bedrock for this system: if all generative models are deleted, the narrative universe must remain consistent with respect to its declared constraints within the relational ledger. The critical caveat to append here is the boundary of generated artifacts: while the narrative state is model-independent, the rendered plates and audio are archive-dependent and cannot be regenerated bit-for-bit, meaning the archive itself is irreplaceable and requires rigorous backup and scrubbing.

The control-plane isolation remains the strongest defense mechanism in the design. Keeping arbitrary-code runtimes entirely separate from the memory space holding elevated GitHub App tokens (using RS256 JWTs exchanged for cached, short-lived installation tokens) halts credential exfiltration. Furthermore, observability independence ensures that the edge controller reporting a GPU failure is not hosted on the hardware that just crashed.

Authentication and idempotency are correctly modeled at the edge. Utilizing HMAC-SHA256 with constant-time comparison and a $\pm5$ minute replay window for webhooks ensures payload integrity. Relying on Cloudflare D1 with an atomic `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and a row-count check eliminates the race conditions inherent in eventually consistent KV stores.

### Critical Corrections to System State and Fencing

The design introduces several contradictions regarding state ownership, lifecycle management, and storage capabilities that will cause silent failures in production.

* **Single-Owner State and the FSM:** The Finite State Machine lacks a formal transition table and incorrectly assigns state ownership to external actors (like workers or humans). The task's Durable Object (DO) must be the sole owner of all states; D1 is merely a projection written by the DO, and external actors simply request transitions. This single-owner model eliminates bugs where D1 and the DO disagree on whether a task is running or expired. Additionally, `HALTED` requires an exit path (e.g., to `PENDING` upon operator resume) so tasks are not permanently stranded, and `ROLLED_BACK` must be formally defined.
* **Structural Fencing, Not Native R2 Fencing:** Cloudflare R2 does not natively compare application-level epoch tokens on upload. Fencing must be enforced structurally: workers upload artifacts to epoch-scoped, content-addressed keys, and the DO validates the epoch during the promotion/completion call. A zombie worker can write bytes to the bucket, but it can never promote them to the canonical path.
* **Watchdog Alarm Cleanup and Budget Leaks:** When a task exits the `RUNNING` state (e.g., to `VERIFYING` or `MERGED`), the DO *must* call `deleteAlarm()`. If left armed, the 30-second watchdog will fire against completed work, expiring the task and triggering duplicate PRs. Furthermore, the alarm handler must explicitly release or settle the budget reservation. Failing to do so means every worker crash permanently leaks reserved budget, eventually halting the system for "exhaustion" while spending nothing.
* **Idempotency Data Loss:** The "claim-before-process" pattern drops events if the isolate crashes after claiming the key but before executing the work, as GitHub will see a 200/202 and not redeliver. This requires a two-phase `RECEIVED` $\to$ `PROCESSING` $\to$ `COMPLETED` flow, accompanied by a reclaim timeout for stuck `PROCESSING` rows.
* **Ledger-Sourced Schema Validation:** Rejecting arbitrary frame counts at the schema layer requires the `duration_ms` and `native_fps` to evaluate the math. If an agent supplies these variables, it can bypass the frame constraints by forging the audio duration. The validation schema must pull these variables directly from the server-side ledger.
* **AST Consistency:** Validating the discrete motor-action array via $O(\min(n, m))$ set-intersection is efficient, but it assumes the array faithfully summarizes the generated prose. An agent can easily output `["LIMP"]` in the array while writing that the character sprinted. A consistency check between the independently extracted prose actions and the declared array is required.

### Restoring Lost Mechanics

Several high-value mechanics established in prior iterations were dropped and must be reinstated:

* **The Merge and Quality-Result Handler:** A dedicated handler is required to receive the quality-gauntlet results and drive the transition from `VERIFYING` to `MERGED`, `RETRYING`, or `AWAITING_APPROVAL`.
* **SHA-Pinned Merging:** To prevent time-of-check-to-time-of-use races, the merge execution must re-fetch the PR, verify the head SHA matches the audited SHA, confirm required checks are green, and pass the `sha` parameter to the GitHub merge API so it rejects updates if the branch has moved.
* **Strict Approval Mechanics:** Slack interactive payloads arrive form-encoded, not as raw JSON. Approval buttons must be bound to a specific `(task_id, head_sha)`, verified against a user allowlist on the callback, consume the approval idempotently, and be backed by a 24-hour timeout owner.
* **The Fail-Loud Mandate:** The strict ban on mock templates and simulated job IDs must be enforced; silent fallbacks mask failures until final review, which is the most expensive time to discover them.
* **Cron Restorations:** The hourly reconciler, daily sweeper, monthly canary, and idempotency-table retention purges must be registered and active to maintain system health.
* **Full Lease Path on Retry:** When a task enters `RETRYING`, it must acquire a fresh lease, a new epoch, a new branch, and a fresh budget reservation, rather than reusing an old epoch and running with fenced-out authority.

### Worthy Additions for Production Resilience

To elevate this architecture from a design document to a deployable system, several operational realities must be introduced:

* **The Saga Outbox Pattern:** Sagas executed in a single request are vulnerable to partial failures. Instead of writing to D1 and calling GitHub sequentially, record the intended compensating actions (e.g., `CLOSE_PR`, `DELETE_REF`, `RELEASE_BUDGET`) in the DO's durable storage. An alarm-driven executor can then retry these actions idempotently, transforming the saga from "best effort" into a guaranteed "eventually completes" model.
* **The Single Contract of Record:** The transition table, the D1 DDL with migrations, and the Zod dispatch contracts should be written as executable code with exhaustive property tests. Prose documentation should derive from these artifacts, not the other way around.
* **Explicit Failure-Mode Matrices:** Define the exact behavior (what halts, what continues, what alerts) when dependencies fail. For example, if the `GlobalCoordinator` DO is unreachable, tasks must have a defined fail-safe (e.g., cache system status in the task DO for a few seconds) to prevent a correlated failure where all leases expire simultaneously.
* **Shadow Mode Rollout:** Implement a mode flag that wraps every mutating GitHub API call. Run the audit engine in shadow mode to log advisory checks against real agent PRs for several weeks. This allows tuning of the substring firewalls and regex protections before a false positive destroys a legitimate branch.
* **Clarified Deployment Tier:** The design oscillates between a solo-operator setup and a highly collaborative distributed system. Acknowledge that features like distributed leases, fencing, and sagas are collaborative-tier mechanics. For a solo tier, server-authoritative attempt counting, fail-loud dispatch, content-addressed archiving, and daily budget caps are sufficient.The era of iterative prose design for this control plane is complete; the immediate mandate is the construction of executable artifacts—specifically the state machine transition table, the D1 Data Definition Language (DDL) with migrations, and the Zod dispatch contracts. The transition from architectural theory to a resilient system requires acknowledging the limits of distributed coordination and enforcing rigorous, unified choke points.

### I. The Validated Architectural Core

* The Deletion Principle establishes that narrative state is model-independent truth housed in the ledger. Rendered plates and audio are archive-dependent artifacts that cannot be regenerated bit-for-bit, meaning the archive itself is irreplaceable and requires active backup strategies. Ledger consistency is solely dependent on the completeness of its explicitly declared constraints.
* Control-plane isolation prevents arbitrary-code runtimes from compromising environments. Elevated GitHub App tokens are protected by minting cached, short-lived installation tokens strictly on demand at the edge. Observability independence ensures the reporting controller does not crash alongside the GPU.
* Atomic idempotency utilizes a two-phase `RECEIVED` to `PROCESSING` to `COMPLETED` lifecycle. This flow is paired with a reclaim timeout for crashed tasks to ensure events are neither duplicated nor lost.
* The Durable Object (DO) serves as the single-owner of task state, pushing updates to D1 merely as a projection to eliminate cross-database disagreement bugs.
* Structural fencing relies on epoch-scoped keys for artifact uploads. The DO validates the epoch upon promotion, ensuring a zombie worker can write bytes to storage but can never promote them to the canonical path.
* Server-sourced facts prevent client-side bypasses by extracting variables like `duration_ms` and `native_fps` directly from the ledger rather than trusting agent requests.
* The outbox pattern durably records intended compensating actions, allowing an alarm-driven executor to retry them idempotently and guarantee eventual saga completion.
* Secure merge mechanics mandate re-fetching the PR, comparing the head SHA to the audited SHA, and merging explicitly with the `sha` parameter to prevent time-of-check-to-time-of-use injection races.

### II. Crucial Edge Cases & Engineering Realities

* Because D1 is merely a projection, it cannot be used to gate actions like deduplication or budget checks. D1 remains strictly necessary for cross-task queries and the reconciliation loop. To maintain eventual consistency, the DO must write to the D1 projection exclusively via its outbox.
* Structural fencing only remains secure if DO promotion is the absolute exclusive pathway to canonical storage. Abandoned zombie writes necessitate a garbage collector to reap staging objects that lack a corresponding DO promotion record.
* A DO possesses only one alarm slot, requiring a single internal alarm scheduler to maintain a sorted list of pending timers in storage and dispatch them by type. Alarm handlers must be strictly idempotent and re-read state upon firing.
* GitHub does not dependably redeliver failed webhooks, shifting the burden of catching dropped events entirely to the reconciler. Reclaiming a `PROCESSING` row is only safe if the underlying handlers are fully idempotent.
* Validating prose against dual-field AST arrays provides two noisy, independent signals rather than absolute certainty. Disagreement correctly triggers a review, while agreement requires empirical measurement of the extractor's actual miss rate.
* The "solo tier" cannot skip core safety mechanisms; it still explicitly requires a kill switch, per-scene spend ceilings, dispatch-call idempotency, endpoint authentication, backup verification, and lightweight heartbeats.

### III. The Missing Operational Glue

* A universal `leaveRunning(reason)` choke point is mandatory. Scattering cleanup logic across the codebase guarantees a skipped step; this single function must execute alarm cleanup, budget settlement, outbox enqueue, and projection updates for every exit state (e.g., success, rollback, timeout, manual cancel).
* Budget settlement math requires a defined policy for crashed jobs where the exact GPU consumption is unknown. Conservative charging—billing the fully reserved amount—acts as the safest default for the daily cap.
* Time authority must be explicitly mapped: the DO's clock governs leases, the Worker's clock governs replay windows, and a designated timezone governs daily budget rollovers.
* Human-in-the-loop workflows need explicit failure pathways, such as escalating, automatically extending, or failing-closed when an approver is unavailable, paired with rate-limited notifications.
* Every task record must include a `contract_version` to safely route in-flight tasks when schemas or execution logic inevitably migrate.
* An append-only decision log is required to prevent repeating historical design regressions. A claims ledger must accompany the architecture, tagging every assertion explicitly as designed, implemented, or measured.
* The control plane's own interface must be secured. Destructive actions require confirmation loops, logged identities, and a break-glass procedure that functions when Slack is down.

### IV. Worthy Additions & Immediate Next Steps

To transition this architecture from theory to runtime, the following additions bridge the gap between design and telemetry:

* **The "Shadow Mode" Telemetry Sink:** When running the audit engine in shadow mode, failed invariant checks should not merely log to standard output. They should write to a dedicated `shadow_violations` D1 table. This builds an empirical dataset to measure the false-positive rate of your substring firewalls and negation-parsers before turning on destructive rollbacks.
* **Out-of-Band Break-Glass UI:** Because Slack is the primary gateway for the kill switch and approvals, a Slack outage represents a critical loss of control during a runaway agent loop. Deploy a minimalistic, zero-dependency Cloudflare Pages dashboard authenticated via Cloudflare Access (Zero Trust) that wires directly to the GlobalCoordinator DO to flip the `master_kill_switch` out-of-band.
* **Cost-Tagging by Contract Version:** Append the `contract_version` and the `model_id` to the `operational_telemetry` table. This allows the reconciler to generate reports showing exactly how much a specific schema migration or prompt adjustment increased or decreased the average per-shot GPU spend.

The immediate execution path requires writing the executable artifacts. First, codify the transition table as a TypeScript mapping with an exhaustive property test. Second, write the single `leaveRunning(reason)` choke point bundled with the DO's priority-queue alarm scheduler. Finally, draft the exact Zod `.refine()` schemas for the dispatch contract, linking them to server-side ledger lookups for dimensions and frame rates.### 1. Epistemic Foundations & The Artifact-First Mandate

The architectural discourse has reached the limit of prose design. Continued iterative refinement of abstract design documents acts as an avoidance mechanism against confronting production failures. System guarantees do not emerge from adjectives like "battle-tested" or "mathematically sound"; they are enforced solely by executable transition matrices, database constraints, and cryptographically signed network contracts.

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      THE CANONICAL SOURCE SPLIT                        │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. THE NARRATIVE LEDGER (Model-Independent Truth)                      │
│    • Stored in relational schemas with foreign keys & check constraints│
│    • Consistent with respect to declared constraints                   │
│    • Survives the complete deletion of all generative AI models       │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. THE MEDIA ARCHIVE (Archive-Dependent Artifacts)                     │
│    • Generated video latents, keyed plates, and audio stems            │
│    • Irreplaceable: cannot be reproduced bit-for-bit from seeds       │
│    • Must be content-addressed, multi-cloud backed, and scrubbed       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

#### The Deletion Principle Boundary

The Deletion Principle governs narrative state: *If every generative model (LLM, diffusion checkpoint, voice model) is permanently deleted, the universe remains logically consistent within the relational ledger with respect to its declared constraints.*

However, this principle carries a physical boundary: **generated media assets are archive-dependent**. Because latent sampling, floating-point GPU variance, and non-deterministic CUDA kernels prevent bit-identical regeneration of diffusion plates and audio stems, the archive is irreplaceable.

The story is model-independent (ledger); the footage is archive-dependent (content-addressed storage). A complete recovery policy mandates:

* Append-only content-addressed object storage (Cloudflare R2) mirrored asynchronously to an independent secondary cold provider.
* Automated weekly scrubbing drills: calculating cryptographic checksums over a random 5% sample of stored media to detect bit rot.
* Monthly cold-restore drills: restoring an entire historical scene assembly from raw archive bytes into a clean environment to verify asset-to-manifest integrity.

### 2. Authority Partitioning & The Deduplication Architecture

A critical failure in distributed systems is conflating edge-level transport idempotency with task-level execution authority. The system resolves this by establishing clear boundaries between Cloudflare D1 and Durable Objects (DO).

```text
[ INBOUND WEBHOOK / CHATOPS ]
              │
              ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ EDGE LEVEL: TRANSPORT IDEMPOTENCY (Authoritative: Cloudflare D1)       │
│                                                                        │
│ • Keyed on: (source, delivery_id)                                      │
│ • State: RECEIVED -> PROCESSING -> COMPLETED                           │
│ • Insert: INSERT INTO idempotency_keys ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING      │
│ • Concurrency Defense: Lease timeout on PROCESSING rows                │
└─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │ Valid & Unique
                              ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TASK LEVEL: STATE, TIME, & BUDGET (Authoritative: Durable Objects)     │
│                                                                        │
│ • GlobalCoordinator DO: Singleton owning daily budget reservations    │
│ • ShotCoordinator DO: Instance per task owning FSM, epoch, & timers   │
│ • D1 Task Rows: Passively updated projections via DO Outbox            │
│ • Enforcement Rule: Gating decisions MUST read DO; never read D1       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

#### Authority Partitioning Rules

* **D1 is Authoritative for Transport Deduplication:** Webhook deliveries from GitHub, Slack, or RunPod arrive at the edge before a task exists. The D1 `idempotency_keys` table is the authoritative arbiter of delivery uniqueness. Using atomic `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, duplicate network transmissions are rejected at the edge isolate.
* **Durable Objects are Authoritative for Task State:** The `ShotCoordinator` DO is the sole owner of a task's lifecycle, monotonic epoch, and active timers. The `GlobalCoordinator` DO is the sole owner of the studio's in-flight spend ledger and master kill switch. D1 execution rows are read-only projections updated asynchronously.
* **Drift Reconciliation:** Network boundaries make instantaneous cross-store consistency impossible. Disagreement between DO memory and D1 rows is transient and repairable. All operational gates (merging, dispatching, spending, renewing) read directly from the DO. The background reconciler queries D1 projections to identify stale or orphaned tasks, using the DO as the ultimate source of truth to heal drift.

#### Two-Phase Idempotency with Concurrency Protection

The "claim-before-process" pattern risks dropping events if the isolate crashes while work is scheduled. Transport idempotency enforces a guarded, three-stage lifecycle:

```sql
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  scope TEXT NOT NULL,
  status TEXT CHECK(status IN ('RECEIVED', 'PROCESSING', 'COMPLETED', 'FAILED')) NOT NULL,
  handler_lease_expires_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
  response_payload TEXT,
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
  updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL
);

```

1. **Ingress (`RECEIVED`):** The webhook delivery ID is inserted with a short `handler_lease_expires_at` timestamp ($T_{\text{now}} + 60\text{s}$). If the key exists and `status === 'COMPLETED'`, the cached response is returned immediately.
2. **Processing (`PROCESSING`):** The edge isolates update `status = 'PROCESSING'`. If a catastrophic isolate failure occurs mid-execution, GitHub does not reliably redeliver. The reconciler daemon scans for rows stuck in `PROCESSING` whose `handler_lease_expires_at < now`.
3. **Reclaim & Replay Safety:** A stuck row can only be reclaimed if the downstream handler is verified as replay-safe (converges on the same final state upon rerun). Handlers check existing state before dispatching: verifying if a Check Run already exists for the head SHA or if an artifact is already staged before performing side effects. Once work finishes, the row updates to `COMPLETED`.

### 3. The Unified Choke Point: `leaveRunning()` & The Alarm Scheduler

Scattering state changes, budget reconciliations, timer cancellations, and projection updates across disparate error handlers guarantees an execution path that skips cleanup. Every exit from the `RUNNING` state must pass through a single, strictly typed choke point inside the `ShotCoordinator` DO.

#### The Closed Exit Reason Enum

`leaveRunning` accepts only an exhaustive, closed set of exit reasons. Adding a new failure mode requires updating this enum and explicitly defining its cleanup semantics:

```typescript
export type ExitReason =
  | 'SUCCESS_MERGE'           // PR passed all gates and merged to main
  | 'QUALITY_RETRY'            // Failed lint/test; attempts < max; convergent trajectory
  | 'SECURITY_ROLLBACK'       // Tampering, path escape, ancestry rewrite, or whitelist breach
  | 'WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT'        // Worker failed to send heartbeat within lease window
  | 'ABSOLUTE_TIMEOUT'        // Worker alive but exceeded maximum task ceiling (15m)
  | 'KILL_SWITCH_HALT'        // Administrative emergency halt triggered
  | 'BUDGET_EXHAUSTED'        // Daily spend limit exceeded during execution
  | 'APPROVAL_REJECTED'       // Human Lead Architect explicitly clicked Reject
  | 'APPROVAL_TIMEOUT'        // Human approval card expired after 24 hours
  | 'OPERATOR_CANCEL'         // Interactive manual cancellation via ChatOps
  | 'WORKER_ABORT'            // Worker gracefully reported internal unrecoverable failure
  | 'RECONCILER_EXPIRY'       // Background reconciler purged an abandoned or orphaned task
  | 'DLQ_TERMINAL';           // Retry limit breached or divergent error oscillation

```

#### The `leaveRunning()` Functional Contract

`leaveRunning` performs in-memory state updates and delegates all external network interactions to an outbox:

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               leaveRunning(reason, payload) CHOKE POINT                │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. ASSERT STATE: Validate currentState === 'RUNNING'                   │
│ 2. CANCEL TIMERS: Remove 'WATCHDOG' & 'ABSOLUTE_CAP' from Scheduler    │
│ 3. BUMP EPOCH: Increment epoch counter to fence out in-flight writes   │
│ 4. SET TERMINAL/NEXT STATE: Transition to next legal FSM state         │
│ 5. SETTLE BUDGET: Settle actual spend or release full reservation      │
│ 6. ENQUEUE OUTBOX: Persist compensating side effects into DO Storage   │
│ 7. FLUSH OUTBOX: Trigger outbox processor to drain network calls       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

#### Priority-Queue Alarm Scheduler inside the Durable Object

A Durable Object possesses exactly one hardware alarm slot (`storage.setAlarm()`). Calling `deleteAlarm()` to stop a watchdog cancels all other active timers on that object (such as a 24-hour approval timer or an absolute task ceiling). The DO must manage timers via an internal priority-queue scheduler:

```typescript
export interface ScheduledTimer {
  id: string;
  type: 'WATCHDOG' | 'ABSOLUTE_CAP' | 'APPROVAL_TIMEOUT' | 'OUTBOX_DRAIN';
  epoch: number;
  fireAt: number;
}

export class TimerScheduler {
  constructor(private storage: DurableObjectStorage) {}

  async schedule(timer: ScheduledTimer): Promise<void> {
    const timers = (await this.storage.get<ScheduledTimer[]>('scheduled_timers')) || [];
    // Remove existing timer of same ID if updating
    const filtered = timers.filter(t => t.id !== timer.id);
    filtered.push(timer);
    filtered.sort((a, b) => a.fireAt - b.fireAt);
    
    await this.storage.put('scheduled_timers', filtered);
    // Arm hardware alarm to the earliest due timer
    await this.storage.setAlarm(filtered[0].fireAt);
  }

  async cancel(timerId: string): Promise<void> {
    const timers = (await this.storage.get<ScheduledTimer[]>('scheduled_timers')) || [];
    const filtered = timers.filter(t => t.id !== timerId);
    await this.storage.put('scheduled_timers', filtered);

    if (filtered.length === 0) {
      await this.storage.deleteAlarm();
    } else {
      // Re-arm hardware alarm to next earliest
      await this.storage.setAlarm(filtered[0].fireAt);
    }
  }

  async getDueTimers(currentEpoch: number): Promise<ScheduledTimer[]> {
    const now = Date.now();
    const timers = (await this.storage.get<ScheduledTimer[]>('scheduled_timers')) || [];
    const due: ScheduledTimer[] = [];
    const remaining: ScheduledTimer[] = [];

    for (const t of timers) {
      if (t.fireAt <= now) {
        // Discard stale timers created under previous epochs
        if (t.epoch === currentEpoch) {
          due.push(t);
        }
      } else {
        remaining.push(t);
      }
    }

    await this.storage.put('scheduled_timers', remaining);
    if (remaining.length > 0) {
      await this.storage.setAlarm(remaining[0].fireAt);
    } else {
      await this.storage.deleteAlarm();
    }

    return due;
  }
}

```

### 4. Financial Safety: Dual-Ledger Settlement & The Outbox Pattern

#### Dual-Ledger Cost Accounting

Conservative charging (billing the full reserved compute budget upon worker crash or timeout) protects the studio from runaway financial leaks. However, logging conservative estimates as factual expenses corrupts telemetry. The architecture implements a **Dual-Ledger Accounting Model**:

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        DUAL-LEDGER COST MODEL                          │
├──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LEDGER A: THE HARD SPEND CAP     │ LEDGER B: AUDIT & TELEMETRY         │
│ (GlobalCoordinator In-Memory)    │ (D1 operational_telemetry)          │
├──────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ • Conservative accounting        │ • Best-known actual telemetry       │
│ • Crashed job = full reservation │ • Crashed job = elapsed heartbeat   │
│   charged against daily ceiling  │   duration * tier hardware rate     │
│ • Guarantees financial safety    │ • Prevents false cost inflation in  │
│   under worst-case billing       │   engineering dashboards            │
└──────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘

```

* **Crash-Loop Diagnostic Alerts:** If the daily budget cap trips because of accumulated crash penalties rather than completed work, the system surfaces a specialized P0 alert to Slack:
> `🚨 FINANCIAL CEILING REACHED VIA TASK FAILURES`
> `Daily Cap: $25.00 | Settled Spend: $4.20 | Forfeited Reservations: $20.80`
> `Root Cause: 8 consecutive worker timeouts on Task TASK-04.02 (Rig 2 CUDA OOM). Halting further dispatches.`



#### Durable Outbox Pattern for Asynchronous Sagas

A saga that performs multiple external API calls sequentially inside a single Worker request is fragile. If the Worker isolate is terminated midway through, the saga halts in a partially rolled-back state.

All side effects are committed to the DO's durable storage as an atomic **Outbox Table** before execution:

```typescript
export interface OutboxMessage {
  id: string;
  type: 'GITHUB_CLOSE_PR' | 'GITHUB_DELETE_REF' | 'D1_PROJECTION_UPDATE' | 'GLOBAL_BUDGET_SETTLE';
  payload: Record<string, any>;
  attempts: number;
  nextRetryAt: number;
}

```

* **Execution Guarantee:** The DO's timer scheduler arms an `OUTBOX_DRAIN` alarm. The processor executes each side effect idempotently. If GitHub returns a 500 or rate-limit error, the outbox message is scheduled for exponential backoff retry.
* **Decoupled Failure Domains:** The task's terminal state is committed instantly in DO memory; external network latency or downstream platform outages cannot roll back the local state machine.

### 5. Operational Hardening, Break-Glass, & Security Surface

#### Out-of-Band Break-Glass Architecture

Relying on Slack slash commands for the emergency kill switch introduces a critical failure mode: if Slack experiences an API outage during a runaway agent loop, the operator loses control of the spending pipeline.

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                SECURE BREAK-GLASS ARCHITECTURE                         │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PATH 1: CHATOPS (Primary / Low Friction)                               │
│ • Slack /kill command -> repo-bot Worker -> GlobalCoordinator DO      │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PATH 2: OUT-OF-BAND ACCESS DASHBOARD (Zero-Dependency Secondary)       │
│ • Cloudflare Pages UI isolated from primary bot worker                 │
│ • Authenticated via Cloudflare Access (Zero Trust SSO)                 │
│ • Edge Worker verifies Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion against public certs   │
│ • Flips master_kill_switch directly on GlobalCoordinator DO           │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PATH 3: NO-CODE MANUAL RUNBOOK (Catastrophic Edge Failure)             │
│ • Step 1: Open GitHub Settings -> Revoke repo-bot App Installation     │
│ • Step 2: Open RunPod / GPU Console -> Revoke API Key                  │
│ • Result: Hardware halts at provider level; all agent auth severed     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

#### Ground-Truth Labeling for Shadow Mode (`shadow_violations`)

Running linters and PR diff audits in "shadow mode" (where violations log warnings but do not execute destructive branch rollbacks) provides value only if human ground truth is systematically recorded:

```sql
CREATE TABLE shadow_violations (
  violation_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  task_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  head_sha TEXT NOT NULL,
  rule_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  rule_version TEXT NOT NULL,
  violating_span TEXT NOT NULL,
  hypothetical_action TEXT CHECK(hypothetical_action IN ('WOULD_ROLLBACK', 'WOULD_BLOCK_MERGE')) NOT NULL,
  human_disposition TEXT CHECK(human_disposition IN ('UNREVIEWED', 'TRUE_POSITIVE', 'FALSE_POSITIVE', 'AMBIGUOUS')) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UNREVIEWED',
  reviewed_by TEXT,
  reviewed_at INTEGER,
  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL
);

```

During the mandatory 14-day shadow-mode rollout, a weekly review reconciles all `UNREVIEWED` entries. Automated rollbacks are enabled only when the measured false-positive rate falls below $1.0\%$ across a minimum sample of 50 agent pull requests.

#### Dual-Key Webhook Secret Rotation

To prevent deployment outages during scheduled security rotations, `repo-bot`'s HMAC validator supports a 24-hour dual-secret grace window:

```typescript
export async function verifyGitHubHMAC(
  env: Env,
  payload: string,
  signature: string
): Promise<boolean> {
  // Primary Active Secret
  const isPrimaryValid = await constantTimeHMACCheck(payload, signature, env.GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET);
  if (isPrimaryValid) return true;

  // Retiring Secret (Grace Window)
  if (env.GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET_RETIRING) {
    return await constantTimeHMACCheck(payload, signature, env.GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET_RETIRING);
  }

  return false;
}

```

#### Shared GitHub Token Bucket Rate Limiter

The background reconciler, the outbox processor, and the live PR audit engine all consume the same 5,000 req/hour GitHub App installation quota. Without rate-limiting, a large reconciliation sweep after a network blip can exhaust the quota, starving high-priority interactive PR audits.

* The `GlobalCoordinator` maintains an in-memory token bucket for external GitHub calls.
* Interactive PR audits are classified as `HIGH_PRIORITY` and consume available tokens immediately.
* Background reconciler queries are classified as `LOW_PRIORITY` and yield whenever available bucket capacity drops below $20\%$, deferring routine sweeps until the budget recovers.

### 6. Executable Artifacts of Record

The following three artifacts represent the definitive, executable source of truth for the `repo-bot` control plane.

#### Artifact 1: The Executable FSM Transition Matrix (`src/fsm/transitions.ts`)

```typescript
export type TaskState =
  | 'PENDING'
  | 'CLAIMED'
  | 'RUNNING'
  | 'VERIFYING'
  | 'AWAITING_APPROVAL'
  | 'MERGED'
  | 'RETRYING'
  | 'ROLLING_BACK'
  | 'ROLLED_BACK'
  | 'DLQ'
  | 'HALTED';

export type FSMEvent =
  | 'LEASE_CLAIMED'
  | 'WORKER_ACK'
  | 'SUBMIT_VERIFICATION'
  | 'SCOPE_PASS_LOW_RISK'
  | 'SCOPE_PASS_HIGH_RISK'
  | 'QUALITY_PASS'
  | 'QUALITY_FAIL_RETRY'
  | 'SECURITY_VIOLATION'
  | 'HUMAN_APPROVE'
  | 'HUMAN_REJECT'
  | 'APPROVAL_TIMEOUT'
  | 'WATCHDOG_EXPIRE'
  | 'KILL_SWITCH_TRIP'
  | 'OPERATOR_RESUME'
  | 'ROLLBACK_COMPLETE'
  | 'RETRY_EXHAUSTED';

export interface TransitionRule {
  from: TaskState;
  event: FSMEvent;
  to: TaskState;
  authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' | 'WORKER' | 'AUDIT_ENGINE' | 'LEAD_ARCHITECT';
}

export const LEGAL_TRANSITIONS: TransitionRule[] = [
  // Dispatch Phase
  { from: 'PENDING', event: 'LEASE_CLAIMED', to: 'CLAIMED', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },
  { from: 'PENDING', event: 'KILL_SWITCH_TRIP', to: 'HALTED', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },
  { from: 'HALTED', event: 'OPERATOR_RESUME', to: 'PENDING', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },

  // Execution Phase
  { from: 'CLAIMED', event: 'WORKER_ACK', to: 'RUNNING', authorizedActor: 'WORKER' },
  { from: 'CLAIMED', event: 'WATCHDOG_EXPIRE', to: 'ROLLING_BACK', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },
  { from: 'RUNNING', event: 'SUBMIT_VERIFICATION', to: 'VERIFYING', authorizedActor: 'WORKER' },
  { from: 'RUNNING', event: 'WATCHDOG_EXPIRE', to: 'ROLLING_BACK', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },
  { from: 'RUNNING', event: 'KILL_SWITCH_TRIP', to: 'ROLLING_BACK', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },

  // Verification & Routing
  { from: 'VERIFYING', event: 'SCOPE_PASS_HIGH_RISK', to: 'AWAITING_APPROVAL', authorizedActor: 'AUDIT_ENGINE' },
  { from: 'VERIFYING', event: 'SCOPE_PASS_LOW_RISK', to: 'MERGED', authorizedActor: 'AUDIT_ENGINE' },
  { from: 'VERIFYING', event: 'QUALITY_FAIL_RETRY', to: 'RETRYING', authorizedActor: 'AUDIT_ENGINE' },
  { from: 'VERIFYING', event: 'SECURITY_VIOLATION', to: 'ROLLING_BACK', authorizedActor: 'AUDIT_ENGINE' },
  { from: 'VERIFYING', event: 'RETRY_EXHAUSTED', to: 'ROLLING_BACK', authorizedActor: 'AUDIT_ENGINE' },

  // Human Gate
  { from: 'AWAITING_APPROVAL', event: 'HUMAN_APPROVE', to: 'MERGED', authorizedActor: 'LEAD_ARCHITECT' },
  { from: 'AWAITING_APPROVAL', event: 'HUMAN_REJECT', to: 'ROLLING_BACK', authorizedActor: 'LEAD_ARCHITECT' },
  { from: 'AWAITING_APPROVAL', event: 'APPROVAL_TIMEOUT', to: 'ROLLING_BACK', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },

  // Rollback & Replay
  { from: 'RETRYING', event: 'LEASE_CLAIMED', to: 'CLAIMED', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },
  { from: 'ROLLING_BACK', event: 'ROLLBACK_COMPLETE', to: 'ROLLED_BACK', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },
  { from: 'ROLLED_BACK', event: 'RETRY_EXHAUSTED', to: 'DLQ', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' },
  { from: 'ROLLED_BACK', event: 'OPERATOR_RESUME', to: 'PENDING', authorizedActor: 'SYSTEM' }
];

export function validateTransition(from: TaskState, event: FSMEvent, actor: string): TaskState {
  const rule = LEGAL_TRANSITIONS.find(t => t.from === from && t.event === event);
  if (!rule) {
    throw new Error(`ILLEGAL_FSM_TRANSITION: Cannot transition from '${from}' via event '${event}'.`);
  }
  if (rule.authorizedActor !== actor && actor !== 'SYSTEM') {
    throw new Error(`UNAUTHORIZED_FSM_ACTOR: Actor '${actor}' cannot invoke event '${event}'. Expected '${rule.authorizedActor}'.`);
  }
  return rule.to;
}

```
