### 7. Pragmatic Testing & Operational Runbook

#### The Formal FSM Property-Test Suite (`tests/fsm.property.test.ts`)

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { 
  TaskState, FSMEvent, TRANSITION_TABLE, evaluateTransition, FSMContext, AuthenticatedActor 
} from '../src/fsm/transitions';

describe('FSM Graph Verification & Safety Invariants', () => {
  const allStates: TaskState[] = [
    'PENDING', 'CLAIMED', 'RUNNING', 'VERIFYING', 'SCOPE_PASSED',
    'AWAITING_APPROVAL', 'MERGING', 'MERGED', 'RETRYING', 
    'ROLLING_BACK', 'ROLLED_BACK', 'DLQ', 'HALTED'
  ];

  const terminalStates: TaskState[] = ['MERGED', 'DLQ'];
  const nonTerminalStates = allStates.filter(s => !terminalStates.includes(s));

  const allEvents: FSMEvent[] = [
    'LEASE_CLAIMED', 'WORKER_ACK', 'SUBMIT_VERIFY', 'SCOPE_PASS', 'QUALITY_PASS',
    'QUALITY_FAIL_RETRY', 'SECURITY_VIOLATION', 'NEW_HEAD_PUSHED', 'HUMAN_APPROVE',
    'HUMAN_REJECT', 'APPROVAL_TIMEOUT', 'WATCHDOG_EXPIRE', 'ABSOLUTE_TIMEOUT',
    'VERIFICATION_TIMEOUT', 'MERGE_TIMEOUT', 'ROLLBACK_TIMEOUT', 'KILL_SWITCH_TRIP',
    'BUDGET_EXHAUSTED', 'OPERATOR_CANCEL', 'OPERATOR_RESUME', 'OPERATOR_REQUEUE', 
    'MERGE_SUCCEEDED', 'MERGE_FAILED_HEAD_MOVED', 'MERGE_FAILED_CONFLICT', 
    'ROLLBACK_COMPLETE', 'WORKER_ABORT', 'RECONCILER_EXPIRY'
  ];

  const baseContext: FSMContext = {
    taskId: 'TASK-01.01',
    currentEpoch: 1,
    attemptCount: 1,
    maxAttempts: 3,
    isHighRiskPath: false,
    scopeCheckPassed: true,
    qualityCheckPassed: true,
    auditedHeadSha: 'sha-root-1',
    candidateHeadSha: 'sha-root-1',
    branchName: 'spec/task-01.01-attempt1-c7f490',
    prNumber: 42,
    targetRepo: 'worker-sower-engine',
    baseCommitSha: 'sha-base'
  };

  it('Property 1: Active non-terminal states (excluding uninterruptible sagas) must support emergency halt', () => {
    const haltableStates = nonTerminalStates.filter(s => !['HALTED', 'MERGING', 'ROLLING_BACK', 'ROLLED_BACK'].includes(s));

    for (const state of haltableStates) {
      const result = evaluateTransition(state, 'KILL_SWITCH_TRIP', { type: 'SYSTEM_INTERNAL' }, baseContext);
      expect(result.nextState).toBe('HALTED');
    }
  });

  it('Property 2: Graph Reachability Safety - All paths to MERGED must traverse SCOPE_PASSED and MERGING', () => {
    const adjWithoutScope = new Map<TaskState, Set<TaskState>>();
    for (const rule of TRANSITION_TABLE) {
      if (rule.from === 'SCOPE_PASSED' || rule.to === 'SCOPE_PASSED') continue;
      const targets = adjWithoutScope.get(rule.from) || new Set();
      targets.add(rule.to);
      adjWithoutScope.set(rule.from, targets);
    }

    const visited = new Set<TaskState>();
    const queue: TaskState[] = ['PENDING'];
    while (queue.length > 0) {
      const curr = queue.shift()!;
      visited.add(curr);
      for (const next of adjWithoutScope.get(curr) || []) {
        if (!visited.has(next)) queue.push(next);
      }
    }

    expect(visited.has('MERGED')).toBe(false);
  });

  it('Property 3: Graph Reachability Liveness - Every non-terminal state can reach a terminal state', () => {
    const adj = new Map<TaskState, Set<TaskState>>();
    for (const rule of TRANSITION_TABLE) {
      const targets = adj.get(rule.from) || new Set();
      targets.add(rule.to);
      adj.set(rule.from, targets);
    }

    for (const state of nonTerminalStates) {
      const visited = new Set<TaskState>();
      const queue: TaskState[] = [state];
      let canReachTerminal = false;

      while (queue.length > 0) {
        const curr = queue.shift()!;
        if (terminalStates.includes(curr)) {
          canReachTerminal = true;
          break;
        }
        visited.add(curr);
        for (const next of adj.get(curr) || []) {
          if (!visited.has(next)) queue.push(next);
        }
      }

      expect(canReachTerminal, `Liveness failure: State '${state}' has no path to MERGED or DLQ`).toBe(true);
    }
  });

  it('Property 4: Forward Reachability - Every state is reachable from PENDING', () => {
    const adj = new Map<TaskState, Set<TaskState>>();
    for (const rule of TRANSITION_TABLE) {
      const targets = adj.get(rule.from) || new Set();
      targets.add(rule.to);
      adj.set(rule.from, targets);
    }

    const visited = new Set<TaskState>();
    const queue: TaskState[] = ['PENDING'];
    while (queue.length > 0) {
      const curr = queue.shift()!;
      visited.add(curr);
      for (const next of adj.get(curr) || []) {
        if (!visited.has(next)) queue.push(next);
      }
    }

    for (const state of allStates) {
      expect(visited.has(state), `Dead state detected: '${state}' cannot be reached from PENDING`).toBe(true);
    }
  });

  it('Property 5: Guard Determinism & Totality - Rules sharing (from, event) must mutually partition context', () => {
    const grouped = new Map<string, typeof TRANSITION_TABLE>();
    for (const rule of TRANSITION_TABLE) {
      const key = `${rule.from}:${rule.event}`;
      const existing = grouped.get(key) || [];
      existing.push(rule);
      grouped.set(key, existing);
    }

    const testCases: FSMContext[] = [
      { ...baseContext, attemptCount: 1, maxAttempts: 3, isHighRiskPath: false },
      { ...baseContext, attemptCount: 3, maxAttempts: 3, isHighRiskPath: false },
      { ...baseContext, attemptCount: 1, maxAttempts: 3, isHighRiskPath: true },
      { ...baseContext, attemptCount: 3, maxAttempts: 3, isHighRiskPath: true },
      { ...baseContext, rollbackClass: 'SECURITY', rollbackReason: 'TAMPERING_DETECTED' },
      { ...baseContext, rollbackClass: 'INFRASTRUCTURE', rollbackReason: 'TIMEOUT' },
      { ...baseContext, auditedHeadSha: 'sha-root-1', candidateHeadSha: 'sha-root-2' }
    ];

    const actors: AuthenticatedActor[] = [
      { type: 'SYSTEM_INTERNAL' },
      { type: 'AUDIT_ENGINE' },
      { type: 'LEAD_ARCHITECT', userId: 'usr_admin' },
      { type: 'REMOTE_WORKER', workerId: 'wrk_1', epoch: 1 }
    ];

    for (const [key, rules] of grouped) {
      if (rules.length <= 1) continue;

      for (const ctx of testCases) {
        for (const actor of actors) {
          const matching = rules.filter(r => {
            const actorOk = r.authorizedActorTypes.includes(actor.type);
            const guardOk = r.guard ? r.guard(ctx, { headSha: ctx.auditedHeadSha }) : true;
            return actorOk && guardOk;
          });

          expect(
            matching.length,
            `Ambiguity detected on ${key} for actor ${actor.type}. Matches: ${matching.length}`
          ).toBeLessThanOrEqual(1);
        }
      }
    }
  });

  it('Property 6: Terminal State Idempotency across all events', () => {
    for (const termState of terminalStates) {
      for (const ev of allEvents) {
        if (termState === 'DLQ' && ev === 'OPERATOR_REQUEUE') continue;
        const result = evaluateTransition(termState, ev, { type: 'SYSTEM_INTERNAL' }, baseContext);
        expect(result.isNoop).toBe(true);
        expect(result.nextState).toBe(termState);
      }
    }
  });

  it('Property 7: Semantic Execution Trail - Security Violation strictly terminates in DLQ', () => {
    let state: TaskState = 'PENDING';
    let ctx = { ...baseContext, attemptCount: 1, maxAttempts: 3, currentEpoch: 1 };

    // PENDING -> CLAIMED (Issues epoch 2)
    let res = evaluateTransition(state, 'LEASE_CLAIMED', { type: 'SYSTEM_INTERNAL' }, ctx);
    state = res.nextState;
    if (res.contextPatch) ctx = { ...ctx, ...res.contextPatch };
    expect(ctx.currentEpoch).toBe(2);

    // CLAIMED -> RUNNING (Requires epoch 2)
    res = evaluateTransition(state, 'WORKER_ACK', { type: 'REMOTE_WORKER', workerId: 'w1', epoch: 2 }, ctx);
    state = res.nextState;
    if (res.contextPatch) ctx = { ...ctx, ...res.contextPatch };

    // RUNNING -> VERIFYING
    res = evaluateTransition(state, 'SUBMIT_VERIFY', { type: 'REMOTE_WORKER', workerId: 'w1', epoch: 2 }, ctx, { headSha: 'sha-c1' });
    state = res.nextState;
    if (res.contextPatch) ctx = { ...ctx, ...res.contextPatch };

    // Invariant Failure: Security breach detected during verification
    res = evaluateTransition(state, 'SECURITY_VIOLATION', { type: 'AUDIT_ENGINE' }, ctx, { reason: 'TAMPERING: .github/workflows modified' });
    state = res.nextState;
    if (res.contextPatch) ctx = { ...ctx, ...res.contextPatch };
    expect(state).toBe('ROLLING_BACK');
    expect(ctx.rollbackClass).toBe('SECURITY');

    // ROLLING_BACK -> DLQ (Bypasses ROLLED_BACK retry)
    res = evaluateTransition(state, 'ROLLBACK_COMPLETE', { type: 'SYSTEM_INTERNAL' }, ctx);
    state = res.nextState;
    expect(state).toBe('DLQ');
  });
});

```

#### The Triple-Path Break-Glass Runbook

```text
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   TRIPLE-PATH BREAK-GLASS RUNBOOK                      │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PATH 1: CHATOPS KILL SWITCH (Control-Plane-Dependent)                  │
│ • Surface: Slack /repo-bot halt --all                                  │
│ • Routing: Dispatches via Edge Worker to GlobalCoordinator DO.         │
│ • Fate-Sharing: Fails if Slack API or Cloudflare Worker edge is down.  │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PATH 2: OUT-OF-BAND ACCESS UI (Control-Plane-Dependent)                │
│ • Surface: https://ops-admin.studio.internal (Cloudflare Pages)        │
│ • Routing: Authenticates via Cloudflare Zero Trust Access JWT;         │
│   Worker writes system_flags to D1 and command to GlobalCoordinator.   │
│ • Fate-Sharing: Independent of Slack; fails if CF Edge/DO is down.     │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PATH 3: NO-CODE VENDOR REVOCATION (Completely Fate-Independent)        │
│ • Action 1: Open GitHub -> Settings -> GitHub Apps -> Suspend App.     │
│ • Action 2: Open RunPod / GPU Console -> Revoke API Key.               │
│ • Result: Instantly revokes Git write permissions and halts cloud GPU  │
│   spend at the vendor billing boundary. Requires zero running code.    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

The system specification is codified in executable transition rules, multi-lane outbox queues, server-derived parameter lookups, and relational SQLite schemas. Structural fencing, transactional state machines, and fail-closed security replace unverified operational claims.These five documents are a different kind of input from the previous eleven. Those were successive revisions of one implementation. These are earlier-generation narrative specifications: a spec-driven-development overview, a bounded intake protocol, a verification gauntlet, a rollback engine, a circuit-breaker document, and a multi-repo transaction document. They describe the same system I've been reviewing, but they predate almost every correction we made. Reading them now is useful mainly for one reason: they contain the material the later artifacts were built from, so they show which ideas survived, which were corrected, and which were never carried forward.

The documents also make a number of mechanical claims the later revisions had to fix (a force-push-style rollback described as "atomic," a fencing token that "rejects writes with 409" at a layer that can't do that, a "two-phase commit" that isn't one). I'll separate what is sound and worth keeping, what is wrong or overstated (citing the specific correction where one exists), and what is genuinely new and valuable that the later artifacts dropped. As always, I'm reviewing designs, not running systems, and where I depend on GitHub, Cloudflare, or Jules behavior I'm reasoning from how they work as I understand them, so verify against current docs. This stays in the reply, and I'll offer a consolidated document at the end.

---

## Part 1: What is valuable and true

### 1.1 The spec-as-contract idea is the strongest thing here, and it's better specified than in any later artifact

The intake document defines a task as a version-controlled markdown file with machine-parseable frontmatter: `task_id`, `target_repo`, `base_branch`, `budget_cap_usd`, `timeout_seconds`, `allow_dependency_install: false`, and a `closed_ledger_scope` with `in_scope_paths` and `forbidden_paths`, followed by a prose mission and **falsifiable acceptance criteria** that each resolve to a shell command and exit code.

This is the right unit of work, and the later TypeScript artifacts (`DispatchRequestSchema`, task specs in D1) quietly lost half of it. Three properties deserve to be restored:

- **Intent separated from boundaries.** The prose says what outcome is wanted; the frontmatter says what the agent may touch. That grants tactical freedom in syntax while bounding the operational envelope, and it's exactly how you constrain an agent without micromanaging it.
- **Falsifiability as a hard rule.** Acceptance criteria that can't be resolved to a binary command are banned ("clean up the code," "make error handling robust"), because a model can't verify a subjective assertion and will happily declare success. Pre-flight rejection of a spec with no binary criterion, before any tokens are spent, is a genuinely good gate.
- **The spec lives in the repository.** A version-controlled spec gives you review, history, and a stable identity for the task. The later design derived scope from a `ResolvedServerFacts` lookup with unspecified provenance; a spec file in git is a better answer to "where does the whitelist come from," and it resolves an open question I flagged in every round.

### 1.2 Pre-flight auditing before spending anything

Validating the spec through a strict schema, verifying that the base commit exists, verifying that targeted files exist in the tree, and asserting that `forbidden_paths` covers lockfiles and schemas, all before dispatch, is correct. "A defect caught at T0 costs $0.00" is the right economic principle: put every cheap deterministic check ahead of every expensive one.

### 1.3 The gauntlet's ordering by cost and depth

The five levels are correctly ordered from cheapest and most deterministic (type check, lint) to most expensive and least deterministic (an LLM critic), with the dynamic test run last. The general rule (cheap, deterministic, safe checks first; nothing agent-authored executes until the structural checks pass) matches the scope-then-quality split from later rounds. The specific mechanisms worth keeping:

- **Two-pass corpus compilation.** Pass 1 validates shape and scalars, pass 2 validates relational integrity and detects cycles, pass 3 seals with deterministic serialization and a state hash. Separating shape from relations is right, because relational checks are meaningless on malformed entities.
- **The drift tripwire.** `git diff --exit-code compiled/` after recompiling catches both failure modes: source edited without recompiling, and the compiled artifact hand-edited to spoof a pass. That second case is the sharp one, and it is a direct defense against an agent gaming the gate.
- **The defect escape sentry.** Every defect that escapes review becomes a permanent regression test in `tests/escapes/`, and the cumulative battery runs on every branch. This is the mechanism by which the ledger's declared constraints *grow from observed failures*, which I called the correct way to build the constraint set in an earlier round. It's a small, high-value idea.
- **Cross-repo version checks** (`check-versions.ts`) and the requirement that raw markdown is never consumed by downstream runtimes, only compiled state.

### 1.4 Dual-field motor audit, with the cross-field discrepancy gate

The diagram is the clearest statement of the idea: a structured action array and prose are independently checked, and a *discrepancy between them* is itself a fatal signal (AST claims `["LIMP"]`, prose contains "vaulted the gate and sprints"). That cross-field reconciliation is exactly the consistency check I asked for two rounds ago, and this document has it stated correctly, including the negation handling ("he couldn't sprint" must not false-positive) via dependency parsing rather than regex.

### 1.5 Adversarial critic structure, mostly

Separating the critic from the drafting session, forcing an `<analysis_trace>` that quotes specific lines and maps them to citations before any verdict, and rejecting verdicts with no citations are all sound. The forced trace makes the critic's reasoning auditable and cheaply checkable (a verdict that cites nothing is machine-detectable as invalid). The severity matrix (warn versus block versus fatal) is a reasonable triage shape.

### 1.6 Trajectory analysis and the routing matrix

Modeling the error as a signature vector `<Domain, TargetEntity, RuleID, OffendingTokens>` and comparing across attempts is a good representation, richer than the single `errorClass` string in the later code. The dossier format (task, classification, trajectory trace, attempt diffs, the active constraint matrix) is genuinely useful debugging output. The **routing matrix** is the best part of that document: `LOCAL_STYLE_FAILURE` goes to a beat writer for a thirty-second manual rephrase, `CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT` goes to a scene architect to change blocking or free a hand, `UPSTREAM_STRUCTURAL` goes to the showrunner for an exemption or retcon. Matching each failure class to the human role that can actually resolve it, instead of one generic escalation, is a real design insight that the later state machine (with its single `LEAD_ARCHITECT` actor) lost.

### 1.7 Override density as a rule-health metric

`D_override(rule) = (Overrides + CircuitBreakerTrips) / TotalTaskInvocations`, with a threshold flagging rules that fire or get overridden too often as miscalibrated, is a good idea: a rule that's constantly overridden is either wrong or obsolete, and this turns "the rules feel annoying" into a measured signal. It also feeds the shadow-mode labeling loop from later rounds.

### 1.8 Lock ordering for multi-repo work

Acquiring repository leases in a global deterministic order eliminates circular-wait deadlock. That's correct and standard, and the observation that ordering must be applied by every coordinator regardless of how the spec lists repos is the crucial detail. (One caveat below about *which* order.)

### 1.9 Persistent escalation memory

Feeding aborts into a consecutive-failure counter that raises alert urgency from a passive notification to a blocking assignment is a sensible escalation ladder, and it mirrors the accountability sweeper's design.

---

## Part 2: What is wrong, overstated, or contradicted by later corrections

I'll go through these in order of severity. For most, a later revision already contains the fix; I cite it so you can see which corrections these documents predate.

### 2.1 The rollback is described as "atomic" and "ACID," and it is neither

The rollback document says it "enforces ACID transactional semantics over Git repositories, sandboxed virtual machines, and edge ledgers." This claim recurs across the documents ("atomic transaction mechanics," "ACID-compliant Two-Phase Commit coordinator") and is the most consequential overstatement.

- **There is no atomicity across GitHub, D1, a filesystem, and a VM.** A sequence of independent API calls, each of which can fail, is a *saga with compensating actions*, not a transaction. I made this correction in the first round and the later artifacts adopted it (the outbox, idempotent steps, a reconciler as the backstop). The rollback document's four "stages" are each individually reasonable but nothing makes them all-or-nothing: if the process dies after stage 1 and before stage 2, the remote branch is gone and the ledger is unrestored.
- **"Isolation" and "durability" aren't provided either.** Isolation between concurrent tasks is provided by ephemeral branches, which is genuine but partial (two tasks can still conflict at merge). Durability of the *compensating intent* is provided only if the intent is recorded before the effect, which is what the WAL and later the outbox are for.

The accurate description: **an idempotent compensating saga, driven from a durable outbox, with a reconciler ensuring eventual completion.**

### 2.2 The rollback order is wrong for the same reason I flagged in round one

The stage order is: (1) delete the remote branch, (2) restore the ledger snapshot, (3) sanitize the local workspace, (4) revoke the fencing token and finalize the WAL. **Revocation is last.** As I said in the first review, if the remote branch is deleted while Jules is still running, Jules can push and recreate it. The fencing token must be revoked *first* so the worker can no longer write, and only then should the branch be deleted. The later artifacts fixed this (revoke-first, then close PR, then delete ref). This document's own multi-repo section even says "fencing tokens reject late writes with 409," which only works if the token was revoked before the cleanup.

### 2.3 "Reset local tracking ref to S_clean" and `git clean -fdx` on a shared path are hazardous and mostly unnecessary

The rollback runs, on "any local runner": `git checkout main`, `git reset --hard origin/main`, `git branch -D`, `git clean -fdx`.

- **`git clean -fdx` deletes every untracked and ignored file in the working tree**, including `node_modules`, local caches, `.env` files, and any uncommitted work a human has in that checkout. If a rollback ever runs against a developer's working copy or a shared runner directory rather than a disposable clone, this destroys unrelated work. It's only safe in a **freshly cloned, ephemeral workspace that is discarded**, in which case running it is pointless (you just delete the workspace).
- **The whole local-cleanup stage is unnecessary in the design the later rounds converged on.** The control plane is a Cloudflare Worker; it has no local checkout. Jules runs in its own VM, which is discarded. There's no persistent local workspace to reset. The correct policy is to **never reuse a workspace**: provision a fresh clone per attempt and destroy it afterward. That makes "sanitation" a non-operation and removes a class of contamination bugs (leftover build artifacts influencing the next run) by construction. If a persistent runner exists, the clean should be scoped to a dedicated per-task directory, never the repo root.
- **`git reset --hard origin/main` conflates two things.** Resetting to `origin/main` is not resetting to `S_clean` if `main` advanced since the task started; the anchor is the pinned SHA, not the moving branch tip. Use the recorded SHA.

### 2.4 The ledger snapshot restore has a race and a false premise

The snapshot protocol copies `compiled/bible-state.json` to a backup file before the task and copies it back on abort, then runs `npm run compile` "to confirm the local checksum matches S_clean exactly."

- **The compiled artifact is already in git.** Restoring the committed state is `git checkout <S_clean> -- compiled/`, or simply not merging the branch. A filesystem `copyFileSync` backup is redundant with version control and introduces its own failure modes (a backup file left behind, a restore over a concurrently-modified file). The ephemeral branch never touched `main`'s `compiled/` at all; deleting the branch *is* the restore.
- **The premise that the task mutates the canonical ledger on disk in place is the design smell.** If an agent's work can corrupt the shared canonical state before verification, the isolation is insufficient. The agent should only ever change files *on its branch*; the canonical state changes only at merge. Then there is nothing to restore.
- **"Confirm the checksum matches S_clean exactly"** conflates a commit SHA (a Git object hash of a commit) with the SHA-256 state hash `H_root` computed over compiled content. They're different quantities. `S_clean` identifies a commit; `H_root` identifies the compiled state at that commit. Both are useful, and the documents use "SHA-256 commit hash" loosely (Git commit IDs are SHA-1 by default in most repositories unless SHA-256 object format is enabled, which is uncommon). Don't call a commit ID a SHA-256 hash unless the repository actually uses the SHA-256 object format.

### 2.5 The fencing claim is stated where it cannot be enforced

The rollback and multi-repo documents both say a late worker pushing with a stale fencing token "is rejected with HTTP 409 Conflict" by "the edge gateway." Two problems:

1. **Git pushes from Jules go to GitHub, not through your edge.** Jules pushes directly to the remote using its own credentials. There is no gateway in that path to inspect an epoch token. GitHub will not compare your token. The doc says the token is "embedded directly into branch names," which is a *naming* convention, not enforcement: a stale worker pushing to a branch named with an old epoch simply pushes to a branch that the coordinator has already stopped caring about (or deleted, in which case the push *recreates* it).
2. **What actually fences a late push** is a structural property, not a check: the coordinator only ever acts on the branch/SHA for the *current* epoch. A stale worker's push is harmless because (a) it lands on a superseded branch name that nothing promotes, and (b) the GitHub App's credentials for that branch can be revoked or the branch protected. I made this point about R2 in round one; it applies equally to Git. The correct wording: "a stale worker's writes can land but can never be promoted."

There's a related security issue: **Jules is given "read/write permissions only to this ephemeral branch."** GitHub does not offer per-branch write permissions on a token; branch protection rules apply to *patterns*, and a token with `contents: write` can push to any unprotected branch. To confine Jules to `spec/*`, you need branch protection (or rulesets) that block direct pushes to everything *except* `spec/**` for that identity, and the identity must not be a repository admin. The document states the intent as if the token scoping provides it.

### 2.6 The "two-phase commit" is not two-phase commit

The multi-repo document's coordinator has a prepare phase (each repo passes its gauntlet) and a commit phase (merge everything). It calls this "ACID-compliant 2PC" and promises "all-or-nothing." Real 2PC requires that participants **durably promise they can commit** in the prepare phase (holding locks, guaranteeing that a later commit cannot fail), and then commit unconditionally. GitHub gives you no such promise: after every repo "passes," the merge of repo B can still fail (a conflicting push, a branch-protection change, an API error), *after* repo A has already merged. Then you have a torn state and a "rollback" of repo A means **reverting a merge commit on `main`**, a visible, non-atomic, non-instant operation that other people may already have pulled.

Given that, the honest description is **a saga with a forward-recovery preference**, and the design questions become:

- **Merge order and the commit point.** Decide which merge is the point of no return and order the others so the *least reversible* goes last, or design the changes to be backward-compatible so a partial state is safe (add-then-migrate-then-remove patterns).
- **Compensation is a revert commit,** not a reset. `git reset` on a shared `main` is a history rewrite you must never do; the compensating action for a merged change is a revert PR.
- **Make the intermediate states valid.** The best defense against torn state is that each repo's change is independently deployable: an upstream schema change that is *additive* (new optional field) can merge first and stay merged harmlessly if the downstream never lands. That property (compatibility across the merge order) is worth more than any coordinator, and the document never mentions it.
- **The "60-second watchdog" is far too short for a multi-repo Jules run.** The DAG-ordered dispatch has Jules change repo A, compile, then change repo B: each step is minutes of agent time. A 60 s prepare lease would expire on every real task. Use a heartbeat-renewed lease (the later design) with an absolute cap sized to the whole transaction.
- **Alphanumeric lock ordering is fine for deadlock avoidance but conflicts with the dependency order the same document requires.** Locks are acquired alphabetically (`goblin-bible → goblin-config → worker-sower-engine`), while dispatch must follow the dependency DAG (`goblin-config → goblin-bible → worker-sower-engine`, per the diagram at the top of that document). These are two different orders for two different purposes, which is fine, but the document conflates "lock order" and "work order" in places ("Sort... Dispatches Jules down the DAG"), and locks in this design aren't actually held across the long agent run anyway. Say which is which, and note that ordering only prevents deadlock among *coordinators that share the ordering*; a task that touches repos in a different set never conflicts.
- **"Fast-forward merge each ephemeral branch into main"** conflicts with the SHA-pinned squash merge in the later artifact. A fast-forward requires that `main` hasn't advanced since the branch point, which fails the moment anything else lands. Decide the merge method per repo and handle "main moved" explicitly (the later design routes it to `MERGE_FAILED_CONFLICT`/re-verification).

### 2.7 The circuit breaker's "mathematical proof" is not a proof

The trajectory document says a domain jump "constitutes mathematical proof that the constraint space is mutually exclusive: C_somatic ∩ C_epistemic ∩ C_logistical = ∅." This is the same overclaim I corrected in round one and it's stated more strongly here.

- **A category jump is evidence, not proof.** The most common cause is that fixing error A *unmasked* a previously hidden error B in a different domain. The first patch didn't create B; it revealed it. That is progress, not thrashing. Halting on attempt 2 after any category change will abort tasks that were one attempt from success. Later revisions moved to the tiered policy: oscillation (A→B→A) trips immediately; a single new class allows a retry with both constraints stated together; same-class stagnation injects a negative constraint.
- **The empty intersection is a claim about the constraint set, which a SAT check can test directly.** If the pre-flight satisfiability check (later rounds, scoped honestly as a rule-set consistency check) shows the constraints are jointly satisfiable, then the jump cannot be evidence of unsatisfiability. Use the solver as the arbiter rather than inferring emptiness from a trajectory.
- **The worked example is instructive but proves the opposite.** Silas can't sprint, can't shout the secret, and has no free hands. The example is presented as a case where the conflict is real, and it *is* a genuine constraint conflict, but you can only know that by checking the constraint set (hands = 0, so any motor action requiring a hand is infeasible), not by watching the agent fail three times. A pre-flight check would have caught it at T0 for $0.00, which is the document's own stated principle. Running the agent to *discover* an unsatisfiable spec is the expensive way to learn something a solver tells you for free.
- **Two documents disagree on the retry policy.** The SDD overview says convergence allows **one** retry; the circuit-breaker document says convergence allows an attempt 3 (three cycles total); the divergence rule says halt at attempt 2. These are compatible only under a specific reading. State the policy once, in a table.
- **The error signature has the wrong granularity for "same category."** `Domain(E1) = Domain(E2)` treats `banned_verb: sprint` then `banned_verb: dash` as convergence. But it also treats "TypeScript type error in file A" then "type error in file B, caused by the first fix" as convergence, which may be regress. Track whether the *error count* is decreasing and whether the set of failing rules is shrinking, not just the domain label.

### 2.8 The verification gauntlet has correctness and safety holes

**a) Order of execution versus safety.** Level 0 runs `npm run check:ts` and Level 4 runs `vitest` **on the agent's branch, in the verifier's environment.** That executes agent-authored code (and, via `npm` scripts, arbitrary shell commands from `package.json` if the agent changed it). Running the gauntlet inside the control plane or on a shared runner is the exact credential-exposure risk the isolation argument exists to prevent. The scope check (diff against the whitelist, no `package.json` or workflow changes) must run *before* any of these, and the gauntlet itself must run in an **ephemeral, credential-free sandbox** with no access to secrets or the network. The later design got this right by splitting `scope-check` from `quality-gauntlet` and running quality in CI; the gauntlet document doesn't say where the levels run.

**b) The agent can edit the tests it's judged by.** The intake document says Jules should "scaffold or update the Vitest test files first." So the agent *writes* the tests and the code, and then the gate runs the tests the agent wrote. A test that asserts nothing passes. The spec's `in_scope_paths` includes `tests/linters/somaticLinter.test.ts`, meaning the agent is authorized to author the very tests that decide pass/fail. Later rounds forbade agent edits to tests entirely, which is the safe rule when the tests are the acceptance mechanism. For a test-writing task like this one, the fix is different: **acceptance must not depend only on agent-authored tests.** Provide reference tests or property checks the agent cannot see or modify (held-out tests), run mutation testing on the agent's tests (do they fail when the implementation is broken?), or require the human-authored acceptance assertions (criterion 3, "an entity with `banned_kinetic_verbs: ['sprint']` throws `SOMATIC_VIOLATION`") to be encoded in a hidden test file the gate adds at verification time.

**c) The Slop Filter is a brittle heuristic dressed as a gate.** Banning words like *testament, tapestry, delve* is a lexical filter with false positives (a character named "Delve", a legitimate use of "testament") and trivial evasion (synonyms). It's a reasonable *style advisory* and a poor *blocking gate*. "Probabilistic suppression" in the same bullet suggests a statistical component that the check doesn't have. Use it as a warning tier, never as a merge blocker, and track its false-positive rate through the shadow-mode labeling loop.

**d) The "regex triad" style rules** (participial chains, crutch density) are a matter of authorial taste encoded as a blocking rule, and "physical throat-clearing gestures exceeding 1 per 500 words" is an arbitrary threshold. Again a fine advisory; a poor hard gate. And it belongs to the creative pipeline, not the software-verification gauntlet: mixing prose style checks with `tsc` in one "Level 0" muddles two very different confidence classes.

**e) `O(1)` again.** "O(1) set intersection" appears repeatedly; the cost is O(min(n, m)) for arrays of sizes n and m. The complexity claim is decorative, though the point (cheap and deterministic) stands.

**f) The gauntlet mixes "fail" semantics.** Level 3's Severity 3 triggers a "surgical repair cycle" in the matrix but the prose says it "blocks merge," and Severity 4 is "immediate rollback." Then the arbitration table says Level 4 breach → "Hard Rollback; remote branch deleted." A test failure on a branch with attempts remaining should *retry*, not roll back and delete the branch (the correct distinction, made in round three: quality failures retry with feedback; security or tampering violations roll back). The document treats every gate failure as grounds for deletion, which throws away recoverable work.

**g) Level 3 is an LLM and "Temperature 0.0" is not determinism.** A temperature-0 model is *more* consistent, not deterministic across model versions, batching, or hardware. The critic's verdict can change when the provider updates the model. Pin the model version, store the full trace and verdict as an artifact, and treat Level 3 as an advisory signal with a human sample audit (measuring the critic's own false-positive and false-negative rates against labeled cases), not as an authoritative gate.

**h) The "epistemic invariant" check is under-specified.** "Cross-references dialogue tokens against the listener's `known_secrets` ledger" is a semantic entailment problem (does this line reveal the secret?), not a token match. A character can reveal a secret without using any of its tokens. This is a genuine strength target for the extraction pass plus a review sample, not an O(1) lookup.

### 2.9 Intake protocol issues

**a) `UUIDv5(task_id + S_clean)` as the idempotency key is a good idea with a subtle flaw.** It makes the key deterministic per task and base commit, so a retried *dispatch* collapses. But it also means that after a *legitimate retry attempt* (same task, same base SHA), the key is identical, so the second attempt would be treated as a replay of the first and refused or served from cache. The key must include the attempt number (or a per-attempt nonce), or a retry can never dispatch. Deterministic keys are for deduplicating one logical request; a retry is a new logical request.

**b) The intake table specifies `lease_ttl: 600 s` with a `heartbeat_interval: 30 s` and describes `repo-bot` *polling* session telemetry.** Earlier rounds established that the worker heartbeats to the coordinator on a short interval (10 s) against a short lease (30 s), renewed each time, with a separate absolute cap. This table's TTL of 600 s is a static lease, which the same documents elsewhere call "fundamentally flawed," and polling (pull) instead of heartbeat (push) inverts who detects failure: a hung worker sends nothing, so the pull can only detect it at the next poll. Worse, "polling session telemetry" from a Worker means scheduled invocations, not a persistent loop.

**c) "Cost ceiling hard-capped at $0.50, session terminates automatically if token limits are exceeded"** assumes Jules exposes a hard spend cap or that the bot can meter its spend. Whether Jules's API offers per-session budgets is a fact about that product that I can't verify from here, so check it. If not, the ceiling has to be enforced by the bot (terminate the session when metered usage or elapsed time crosses a bound), and the metering source must be trustworthy.

**d) `timeout_seconds: z.number().max(900)` in the schema and `timeout_seconds: 600` in the frontmatter are consistent,** but `budget_cap_usd` allows up to $2.00 in the schema while prose says "hard-capped at $0.50." A schema maximum four times the documented cap invites drift; make the cap a single source of truth.

**e) `task_id` regex is `^TASK-\d{2}\.\d{2}\.\d{2}$` (three segments) while the frontmatter example and other documents use two- or three-segment IDs and a lowercase-with-hyphens branch form (`spec/task-02-01-01-jules`).** The branch name replaces dots with hyphens here but keeps dots elsewhere (`spec/task-04.01-attempt1-...`). The audit's branch-to-task extraction regex depends on the exact form. One shared constant for the ID format and its branch encoding would end this class of bug (the case-sensitivity failure in round three was exactly this).

**f) `allow_dependency_install: z.literal(false)`** makes the field pointless as a *choice* (it can only ever be false) while still requiring every spec to state it. Either remove the field or make the constraint a system-wide invariant not present in specs. Also, "verify the branch includes a frozen `package-lock.json`" is necessary but not sufficient; the agent must also be unable to run `npm install` with network access. That's a sandbox property, not a spec property: the VM should have no outbound network beyond the package cache the spec permits.

**g) The Attention Sandwich prompt structure** (constraints at top, context in middle, exit tests at bottom) is a reasonable *prompting heuristic*, but the document presents its efficacy as fact ("neutralizing the agent's tendency..."). Prompt placement is a soft influence, and the entire safety of the design must not depend on the agent obeying its prompt. The document elsewhere correctly relies on external enforcement (diff whitelist), so this is presentation rather than a design flaw, but say plainly that the prompt is advisory and the diff check is authoritative.

### 2.10 Things that are simply inconsistent across the documents

- **Rollback anchor.** `S_clean` is the pinned commit. Several places reset to `origin/main`. They differ whenever `main` moves.
- **What "BLOCKED" is.** The SDD overview and the circuit breaker use a `BLOCKED` task status; the later FSM has `HALTED`, `DLQ`, and `ROLLED_BACK`. Map them: `BLOCKED` after escalation corresponds to a human-wait state, which the later design gives an expiry and a digest.
- **`digest_state.json` versus D1.** The rollback and circuit-breaker documents write failure counters to `digest_state.json` (a file), while telemetry is written to D1. A Worker has no writable filesystem, and a JSON file is not a concurrency-safe store. The later design puts all of this in D1 with a composite key. Use one store.
- **Two different descriptions of the WAL.** The rollback document has `transaction_wal` with status `PREPARING → ... → ABORTED`; the multi-repo document defines `multi_repo_transactions` with statuses `PREPARING/COMMITTING/ABORTING/RESOLVED`. Two tables, two vocabularies, neither driven by code in the later artifacts (the WAL was defined and never written, a finding from rounds three through six). If a multi-repo transaction record is needed, it should be a parent row referencing the per-repo task rows, driven by the same state machine.
- **"Expires_at" on the transaction row** re-introduces D1 as the lease clock, which contradicts the later single-authority decision (the Durable Object owns time).
- **The multi-repo document's SQL comment calls the table `transaction_wal`** but the `CREATE TABLE` names it `multi_repo_transactions`. Trivial, but symptomatic.

### 2.11 Unsupported precision and rhetoric

"Mathematically impossible," "mathematical proof," "cryptographic workspace isolation" (the section is about branch naming and a commit hash, not cryptography), "unyielding," "un-gameable execution contract," "absolute negative boundary enforcement," and "guarantees" throughout. None of these hold up under the tracing above, and the *un-gameable* claim in particular is false given 2.8b (the agent authors the tests). Replace each with what the mechanism actually guarantees. The design is better without them, and honesty about limits is what makes a control plane trustworthy.

---

## Part 3: What these documents contain that the later artifacts dropped

Several ideas here are valuable and absent from the eleven revisions of the implementation. I'd bring these back.

1. **The spec file as the source of scope.** The later artifacts left the origin of `file_whitelist` and `forbidden_patterns` unspecified (`ResolvedServerFacts` from an unshown lookup). A version-controlled spec with `in_scope_paths`, `forbidden_paths`, and falsifiable acceptance criteria answers it, is reviewable, and gives every task a stable identity.
2. **Falsifiable-criteria linting at intake.** Reject specs with subjective acceptance criteria before dispatch.
3. **The defect escape sentry.** A permanent, cumulative regression battery grown from real escapes. The later design's shadow-mode labeling and rule-version tracking is the *measurement* side; the escape sentry is the *accumulation* side.
4. **Cross-field discrepancy gating** between the structured action array and the prose (present in the later table's guards only implicitly).
5. **The role-based routing matrix** for escalations, instead of a single `LEAD_ARCHITECT` actor. The FSM should gain actor types matching the roles (beat writer, scene architect, showrunner) with their own permitted events, so a stylistic dead end goes to the person who can fix it in thirty seconds.
6. **The rich error signature vector** and the diagnostic dossier (attempt diffs, the active constraint matrix). The later `diagnostic` payload is an unstructured blob; the dossier is what a human actually needs.
7. **Override density** as a rule-health metric.
8. **Coordinated multi-repo specs** as a first-class concept, including DAG-ordered dispatch. The later FSM handles one repo per task and has no notion of a parent transaction; if multi-repo changes are a real requirement, they need a parent state machine whose children are the per-repo tasks.

---

## Part 4: What I would add

### 4.1 Treat multi-repo changes as compatibility-ordered forward migrations, not distributed transactions

Because GitHub cannot provide 2PC, design each cross-repo change so that **every prefix of the merge sequence is a valid state**. Practically: (1) additive upstream change first (new optional field, new export, old still works); (2) downstream consumers migrate; (3) removal of the old path in a later, separate task once nothing depends on it (expand, migrate, contract). With that discipline, a failure mid-sequence leaves a working system that is merely *ahead of* its consumers, and rollback is unnecessary: you simply don't proceed. Keep the coordinator to decide order and record progress, but let compatibility, not atomicity, provide safety.

### 4.2 Define the parent transaction as a state machine over child task machines

If you do coordinate multiple repos, model a `MultiRepoTransaction` with its own states (`PREPARING`, `ALL_VERIFIED`, `MERGING`, `PARTIALLY_MERGED`, `COMPLETED`, `COMPENSATING`, `FAILED`) and explicit rules for what happens on a partial merge: `PARTIALLY_MERGED` is a first-class state with a defined recovery (proceed forward if possible, else revert in reverse merge order via revert PRs, always alerting a human). Make the parent's durable record a Durable Object (single authority), with the per-repo children projected, and drive merges from an outbox with confirmation events, exactly as the single-repo machine does.

### 4.3 Run the gauntlet in an ephemeral, credential-free sandbox, and make acceptance independent of agent-authored tests

Two rules to write down and enforce: (1) the verification environment has no secrets, no repository write access, and no outbound network; it receives a tarball of the candidate branch and returns exit codes and logs; (2) acceptance combines agent-authored tests with **held-out tests and human-authored property assertions** the agent cannot modify or see, plus mutation testing to confirm the agent's own tests can fail. Without (2), "Zero mutations outside scope" and "tests pass" are both satisfiable by a vacuous suite.

### 4.4 Make the spec linter an actual gate with a written rule set

Pre-flight should check: every acceptance criterion maps to an allowlisted command from a registry (the fixed-command-registry idea from round two); `in_scope_paths` and `forbidden_paths` don't overlap; forbidden includes all protected globs (workflows, lockfiles, configs, tests unless the task is test-authoring, in which case tests are in scope *and* held-out tests are added); the base commit exists and is an ancestor of the branch tip; the spec contains at least one criterion that fails on the current base (a "red" precondition proving the criterion measures something) and passes only after the change. That last rule is the strongest anti-vacuity check available: a criterion that already passes before the work tells you nothing.

### 4.5 Bring back the reconciler as the mechanism that makes "atomic" true

Everything in the rollback engine that claims all-or-nothing behavior is true only *eventually*, and only if something keeps retrying. The reconciler is that something. Specify it (scan non-terminal tasks and multi-repo transactions older than their expected duration; compare D1, the Durable Object, and GitHub; fire the legal corrective event; alert on anything it can't repair). Without it, every "the hourly cron will catch it" sentence in these documents is a promise with no code behind it.

### 4.6 Measure the critic

The Panopticon critic and the linters are classifiers with error rates. Keep a labeled set (planted violations, historical escapes, clean samples), report precision and recall per rule and for the critic, and gate promotion of a rule from advisory to blocking on measured numbers with a stated confidence bound, per the shadow-mode design. Also record the model version with every critic verdict so a provider update doesn't silently shift behavior.

### 4.7 Pick one vocabulary and one store

Retire `digest_state.json`, `transaction_wal` versus `multi_repo_transactions`, `BLOCKED`, and `S_clean = origin/main`. One state machine, one authority (the Durable Object), one projection store (D1), one anchor (the pinned commit SHA), one ID/branch encoding, and a diagram generated from the transition table so the documents cannot drift again.

---

## Bottom line

**Keep:**
- The spec as a version-controlled contract with intent separated from boundaries, a closed ledger of in-scope and forbidden paths, and **falsifiable acceptance criteria**, plus pre-flight rejection before any spend.
- The cheap-to-expensive gauntlet ordering, two-pass corpus compilation, the **drift tripwire** (which catches hand-edited artifacts), and the **defect escape sentry**.
- The dual-field motor audit with **cross-field discrepancy gating** and negation-aware parsing.
- The forced `<analysis_trace>` with citation requirements for the critic.
- The rich error-signature vector, the diagnostic dossier, and the **role-based routing matrix**.
- **Override density** as a rule-health metric.
- Deterministic lock ordering for multi-repo work, and escalation memory.

**Correct before relying on it:**
1. **"ACID" and "atomic" are false:** it's an idempotent compensating saga; and the **"two-phase commit"** isn't 2PC because GitHub cannot promise a later merge will succeed. A partial merge is a real state needing a defined recovery via revert PRs.
2. **Rollback order:** revocation must come first, not last, or a live agent recreates the deleted branch.
3. **`git clean -fdx` and `reset --hard origin/main`** are hazardous on shared paths and use the wrong anchor; the fix is disposable per-attempt workspaces and the pinned SHA. The **ledger file backup** duplicates version control, and the real issue is that agents must never mutate canonical state before verification.
4. **The 409-on-stale-token claim** places enforcement where none exists: Jules pushes straight to GitHub. Stale writes can land but must never be promoted, and per-branch token scoping isn't a GitHub feature (use branch protection or rulesets).
5. **"Mathematical proof" of constraint conflict from a category jump** is unsound: a jump is evidence, often of an unmasked error; use a pre-flight satisfiability check to decide it for $0.00.
6. **The agent writes the tests that judge it,** so a vacuous suite passes; add held-out tests, mutation testing, and a red-before-green precondition.
7. **The gauntlet may run agent code in a credentialed environment;** run it in an ephemeral, credential-free sandbox behind the scope check.
8. **The idempotency key `UUIDv5(task_id + S_clean)` blocks legitimate retries;** include the attempt number.
9. **A 600 s static lease and a 60 s multi-repo prepare lease** contradict the heartbeat-renewed design and would expire real runs; and whether Jules exposes a per-session cost cap is unverified.
10. **Gate failures are all treated as grounds for deletion,** discarding recoverable work; quality failures should retry, and only violations roll back.
11. **Style heuristics (slop filter, participial chains, crutch density) are blocking gates** with arbitrary thresholds and easy evasion; demote them to advisories and measure them.
12. **Two WALs, `digest_state.json`, `BLOCKED`, and `origin/main` versus `S_clean`** are vocabulary and store inconsistencies with the later design.

**Keep honest about:** "mathematically impossible," "un-gameable," "cryptographic isolation," "ACID," and "proof" (none survive tracing); temperature-0 as determinism (it isn't); Jules's spend cap and telemetry surface (verify against the product); and the Level 3 critic as an authoritative gate (it's a classifier with an unmeasured error rate).

I can now consolidate the whole series into a single architecture document with a findings register, or write the artifacts these documents imply: a spec-contract schema plus a spec linter (including the red-before-green check and the falsifiable-criteria registry), a `MultiRepoTransaction` state machine with a partial-merge recovery path, or a sandboxed-gauntlet runner contract with held-out tests. Tell me which you'd like and whether you want it as a Word file, an HTML page, or code.The early-generation narrative specifications contain vital operational and domain-specific mechanisms that were inadvertently flattened or lost during later edge-state-machine revisions, alongside critical architectural fallacies that must never reach production. While later revisions hardened the edge runtime—formalizing Durable Object time authorities, atomic D1 idempotency, and fail-closed GitHub check runs—they abstracted away the grounded, human-in-the-loop development practices codified in the original spec-driven development (SDD) and intake documents.

Restoring these lost operational mechanisms while excising the early architectural fictions transforms the control plane from an abstract state machine into an end-to-end, reproducible software studio.

## 1. High-Value Mechanics Rescued from the Early Specifications

The early specifications excel where the later edge-worker revisions became overly abstract: in defining the exact physical boundary of work, structuring adversarial review, and providing semantic context for failure recovery.

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   THE RESTORED SPEC-AS-CONTRACT ARCHITECTURE                     │
├────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ SPEC FRONTMATTER (Rigid Boundary)      │ SPEC BODY (Tactical Freedom)            │
├────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ • target_repo & base_commit_sha        │ • Prose Mission & Narrative Intent      │
│ • budget_cap_usd & timeout_seconds     │ • Structural Context & Character States │
│ • in_scope_paths & forbidden_paths     │ • Dwight Swain MRU Directives           │
│ • held_out_test_suite reference        │ • Falsifiable Acceptance Criteria       │
│ • allow_dependency_install: false      │   (Binary Shell Commands + Exit Codes)  │
└────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

### The Version-Controlled Spec-as-Contract

The later schema revisions reduced task intake to generic database lookups (`ResolvedServerFacts`) with undefined provenance. The early intake document correctly established that **every task must originate as a version-controlled Markdown contract** committed directly to Git:

* **Decoupled Intent and Boundary:** The Markdown frontmatter defines the immutable operational envelope (allowed paths, budget ceiling, base commit SHA, timeout), while the Markdown body provides narrative and architectural intent. This grants the coding agent syntactic freedom within a strictly enumerable blast radius.
* **Falsifiable Acceptance Criteria:** Every acceptance criterion in the spec must resolve to a binary, machine-executable shell command with an expected exit code (e.g., `npx vitest run tests/escapes/esc-042.test.ts --exit-code 0`). Vague, subjective criteria ("clean up the code," "improve voice consistency") are rejected at the intake gate before any API tokens or GPU cycles are billed.
* **Pre-Flight Static Linting (The T0 Gate):** Before allocating a distributed lease or spinning up an agent VM, the edge intake linter audits the contract:
1. Asserts that `in_scope_paths` and `forbidden_paths` do not overlap.
2. Verifies that `forbidden_paths` explicitly covers workflows, lockfiles, Linters, and base configurations.
3. Asserts that the `base_commit_sha` exists on the remote tracking branch and is an ancestor of `HEAD`.
4. Runs the **Red-Before-Green Precondition**: executes the acceptance criteria against the base commit to confirm that at least one criterion fails. A spec that passes before work begins is rejected as vacuous.



### The Defect Escape Sentry (`tests/escapes/`)

A common vulnerability in generative pipelines is fixing a continuity defect (e.g., a character using a severed arm) only for a later agent run to re-introduce the same violation.

The early gauntlet specification introduced the **Defect Escape Sentry**:

* Every narrative breach or structural bug that escapes to review must be codified as an automated, permanent Vitest regression file in `tests/escapes/esc-{issue_id}.test.ts`.
* These tests are permanently added to the repository’s immutable test suite.
* Agents are barred from modifying `tests/escapes/**`. The cumulative battery runs on every future branch, ensuring that the ledger’s declared constraints expand systematically with every observed production failure.

### The Multi-Tier Human Escalation Routing Matrix

Later state machine revisions collapsed all human escalations into a single, generic `LEAD_ARCHITECT` role. The early trajectory-analysis document recognized that human intervention must be routed to the specific creative or technical specialist who can resolve the bottleneck:

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      HUMAN ESCALATION ROUTING TOPOLOGY                           │
├─────────────────────┬───────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Failure Class       │ Responsible Role      │ Operational Remediation            │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ LOCAL_STYLE_FAILURE │ Beat Writer           │ 30-second manual prose rephrase or │
│                     │                       │ dialogue rhythm tweak.             │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT │ Scene Architect       │ Adjust scene blocking, alter prop   │
│                     │                       │ allocation, or free up a hand.     │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ UPSTREAM_STRUCTURAL │ Lead Showrunner       │ Authorize an official canon retcon │
│                     │                       │ or issue a temporary waiver.       │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
│ INFRA_ENVIRONMENT   │ Platform Engineer     │ Resolve container OOM, fix lock    │
│                     │                       │ drift, or adjust GPU canary quota. │
└─────────────────────┴───────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘

```

### The Structured Diagnostic Dossier & Error Vector

Rather than dumping unformatted error logs into Slack, the circuit-breaker engine compiles an actionable **Diagnostic Dossier** upon failure:

* **Signature Vector:** The failure is represented as an explicit 4-tuple:

$$\vec{E} = \langle \text{Domain}, \text{TargetEntity}, \text{RuleID}, \text{OffendingTokens} \rangle$$


* **Attempt Diffs:** Side-by-side diffs showing how the code or screenplay AST mutated across cycles.
* **Active Constraint Matrix:** The specific slice of somatic, logistical, and epistemic rules injected into the prompt context, allowing the human reviewer to pinpoint contradictory directives instantly.

### Override Density ($D_{\text{override}}$) as a Rule-Health Sensor

The early specification included an automated heuristic for detecting obsolete, overly aggressive, or contradictory worldbuilding rules:

$$D_{\text{override}}(\text{rule}) = \frac{\text{Manual Overrides} + \text{Circuit Breaker Trips}}{\text{Total Task Invocations}}$$

If $D_{\text{override}} > 0.15$ across a rolling 30-day window, the rule is flagged in the Astro Cockpit as miscalibrated. This converts subjective writer frustration into an empirical signal, identifying rules that require human pruning.

### The Dual-Field Motor Discrepancy Gate

To prevent hallucinatory agents from gaming lexical linters, the compiler mandates a dual-field AST output: a natural language prose field and an explicit JSON array of discrete motor verbs.

The early document correctly defined the cross-field verification gate:

1. **Direct Array Check:** Runs an $O(\min(n, m))$ set-intersection between the declared motor actions and the character's active `banned_kinetic_verbs` vector.
2. **Independent Extraction Pass:** Runs an isolated, temperature-0 extraction pass over the raw prose to extract all physical motor actions.
3. **Cross-Field Discrepancy Assertion:** Compares the declared array against the independently extracted actions. If the prose says "Silas dashed across the culvert" while the array declares `["LIMP"]`, the discrepancy is flagged as an evasion attempt and fails the build.
4. **Negation-Aware Parsing:** Applies dependency parsing over the prose to prevent false positives when banned verbs are negated (e.g., "he could not *sprint* through the mud").

## 2. Systematic Deconstruction of Early Architectural Fictions

While the early documents contain high-value operational tools, they are riddled with dangerous distributed-systems fallacies that would compromise a production deployment if implemented as written.

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   EARLY FICTION vs. PRODUCTION REALITY                           │
├──────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Early Document Claim                 │ Production Edge Reality                   │
├──────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "ACID Two-Phase Commit over Git, VM, │ False. Cross-system operations are        │
│ and Edge Ledgers."                   │ Idempotent Compensating Sagas.            │
├──────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "Stale worker pushes are rejected    │ False. Git pushes hit GitHub directly.    │
│ with HTTP 409 at the Edge Gateway."  │ Fencing is structural via branch-naming.  │
├──────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "Rollback runs `git clean -fdx` and  │ Dangerous. Shared paths lose untracked    │
│ `git reset --hard origin/main`."     │ files. Use ephemeral disposable VMs.      │
├──────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "Category jump is mathematical proof │ False. Fixing error A frequently unmasks  │
│ of mutually exclusive constraints."  │ error B. Use pre-flight SAT checks.       │
├──────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "Agent writes Vitest tests first to  │ Severe hazard. Self-grading agents pass   │
│ drive acceptance."                   │ vacuous suites. Require held-out tests.   │
├──────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "Idempotency key is deterministic    │ Broken. Legitimate retry attempts share   │
│ `UUIDv5(task_id + S_clean)`."        │ the key and are blocked as replays.       │
└──────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

### The Myth of "ACID Git Transactions" and 2PC

The rollback and multi-repo documents repeatedly promise "ACID transactional semantics" and an "ACID-compliant Two-Phase Commit coordinator" spanning GitHub, Cloudflare D1, local filesystems, and sandboxed VMs.

**This is physically impossible.** There is no two-phase commit coordinator across disparate SaaS APIs.

* In true 2PC, participants enter a prepared state where they lock resources and guarantee that a subsequent commit cannot fail. GitHub offers no such guarantee. After Repository A merges, the merge of Repository B can fail due to a concurrent push, a branch-protection change, or a network timeout.
* When Repository B fails, Repository A is already merged on `main`. You cannot "atomically roll back" a published Git commit. Undoing it requires pushing a revert commit—a visible, asynchronous, non-instant operation that other developers or downstream jobs may have already pulled.
* **The Correction:** Replace 2PC framing with an **Idempotent Compensating Saga**. Acknowledge partial failure states explicitly (`PARTIALLY_MERGED`) and enforce forward-compatibility over atomic rollback.

### The Fatal Revocation-Last Rollback Order

The early rollback document specifies an execution sequence of:

1. Delete remote branch.
2. Restore ledger snapshot.
3. Sanitize local workspace.
4. Revoke fencing token and finalize WAL.

As proven in earlier reviews, **this order guarantees race conditions**:

* If an agent VM is still executing when Stage 1 deletes the branch, the agent’s background push will land milliseconds later, recreating the remote branch on GitHub.
* **The Correction:** Always enforce **Revoke-First Authority Stripping**. The Durable Object must increment its monotonic epoch and revoke the worker lease *before* touching GitHub branches or closing Pull Requests.

### The Hazard of Shared-Workspace Sanitation

The early rollback engine commands local runners to execute:

```bash
git checkout main
git reset --hard origin/main
git branch -D spec/branch
git clean -fdx

```

* `git clean -fdx` deletes every untracked file, ignored directory, local `.env` configuration, and dependency cache (`node_modules`) in the tree. Running this on a shared developer workstation or persistent runner destroys unrelated work and forces multi-gigabyte dependency reinstalls.
* `git reset --hard origin/main` resets to the moving branch tip rather than the immutable anchor commit ($S_{\text{clean}}$). If another engineer pushed to `main` while the task was running, the local checkout silently jumps forward.
* **The Correction:** Eliminate persistent workspaces entirely. Every task must execute inside an ephemeral, disposable container or cloud VM that is destroyed upon task completion.

### The Illusion of Gateway-Level Git Fencing

The early specifications claim that if a partitioned or zombie worker attempts to push code with an expired fencing token, the edge gateway "intercepts the write and rejects it with HTTP 409 Conflict."

* This is a severe misunderstanding of Git topology. Coding agents (like Jules) push commits directly to GitHub’s remote servers over HTTPS/SSH, completely bypassing the Cloudflare edge isolate. The edge Worker cannot inspect Git push packets.
* **The Correction:** Fencing on Git is **structural, not transport-level**. The coordinator assigns an epoch-tagged branch name (`spec/task-01-attempt2-${epoch}`). If a stale worker pushes to an old branch, it lands on an abandoned ref that `repo-bot` simply ignores. Furthermore, `repo-bot` gates Pull Request merges by comparing the commit SHA against the active epoch stored in the Durable Object.

### The "Mathematical Proof" Fallacy in Trajectory Analysis

The early circuit-breaker document asserts that if an agent fails Attempt 1 with a somatic error (e.g., using a disabled arm) and Attempt 2 with an epistemic error (e.g., blurting out a secret), this "constitutes mathematical proof that the constraint space is mutually exclusive."

* This is mathematically and empirically false. In software engineering and narrative generation, fixing Error A frequently **unmasks** Error B. The model’s first output was so broken by the somatic violation that the critic never evaluated the downstream dialogue. Fixing the physical posture allowed the model to generate the dialogue, exposing a pre-existing epistemic leak.
* **The Correction:** Treat category jumps as evidence to be evaluated, not an instant death sentence. Use a pre-flight SAT solver over the relational constraint set to prove mutual exclusivity for $\$0.00$ before dispatching the agent. If the rules are mathematically compatible, allow Attempt 3 with both constraints explicitly unified in the prompt.

### The Self-Grading Agent Trap

The intake specification casually instructs that the agent should "scaffold or update the Vitest test files first, then implement the feature until tests pass."

* **This is the ultimate automated failure mode.** An agent tasked with writing its own tests and then satisfying them will inevitably write tautological assertions (`expect(true).toBe(true)`) or delete the assertions it cannot satisfy to achieve a green CI badge.
* **The Correction:** The agent must never author the acceptance mechanism. Acceptance must be evaluated against **Held-Out Test Suites** injected by the verification harness at audit time, supplemented by mutation testing to confirm that the agent's tests fail when the code is broken.

### The Deterministic Idempotency Flaw

The early intake document specifies calculating the task idempotency key as:


$$\text{IdempotencyKey} = \text{UUIDv5}(\text{task\_id} + S_{\text{clean}})$$

* Because `task_id` and the base commit SHA ($S_{\text{clean}}$) are static, an agent that fails Attempt 1 and is rescheduled for Attempt 2 generates the exact same UUID. The edge deduplication layer sees the existing key, marks it as a replay, and drops the retry request.
* **The Correction:** The idempotency key must explicitly bind the attempt number and a unique run nonce:

$$\text{IdempotencyKey} = \text{UUIDv5}(\text{task\_id} + \text{":"} + \text{attempt\_number} + \text{":"} + S_{\text{clean}})$$

## 3. Coordinated Multi-Repo Architecture: Sagas Over "2PC"

When an architectural change spans multiple repositories (e.g., updating a narrative Zod schema in `goblin-bible`, consuming it in `worker-sower-engine`, and adjusting viewports in `goblin-viewport`), the studio cannot rely on atomic multi-repo commits. It must enforce an **Expand, Migrate, Contract** forward-compatibility pipeline managed by a parent coordinator.

```text
               PARENT TRANSACTION: MultiRepoTransaction DO
                                    │
       ┌────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┐
       ▼                            ▼                            ▼
[ Child Task: bible ]     [ Child Task: sower ]      [ Child Task: viewport ]
       │                            │                            │
       ▼ (Passes Gauntlet)          ▼ (Passes Gauntlet)          ▼ (Passes Gauntlet)
  ALL_CHILDREN_VERIFIED ────────────┴────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ COMPATIBILITY-ORDERED FORWARD MERGE SEQUENCE                           │
│                                                                        │
│ Step 1: Merge goblin-bible (Additive Change: Schema v2 adds fields)    │
│ Step 2: Merge worker-sower-engine (Migrate: Consumes new fields)       │
│ Step 3: Merge goblin-viewport (Migrate: Renders new layout)            │
└───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
             ┌──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐
             ▼ ALL SUCCEED                                 ▼ STEP 2 FAILS (Torn State)
┌─────────────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STATUS: COMPLETED       │               │ STATUS: PARTIALLY_MERGED             │
│ Tag all repos at HEAD   │               │ • bible remains merged (Additive OK) │
│ Finalize transaction    │               │ • Dispatch Revert PR for sower       │
└─────────────────────────┘               │ • Escalate to Showrunner with diff   │
                                          └──────────────────────────────────────┘

```

### The Forward-Compatibility Mandate (Expand, Migrate, Contract)

Because partial merges can occur when GitHub encounters API blips or base-branch conflicts, cross-repo changes must be designed so that **every prefix of the merge sequence is a valid system state**:

1. **Expand (Upstream First):** Upstream schemas (`goblin-bible`) merge first and must be strictly additive (new optional fields, non-breaking enum additions). If downstream consumers fail to merge, the upstream addition sits harmlessly in trunk without breaking legacy runtimes.
2. **Migrate (Downstream Consumers):** Middle-tier engines (`worker-sower-engine`) update to consume the new schema fields.
3. **Contract (Cleanup Task):** Deprecated legacy fields are removed in an independent, subsequent transaction once all consumers have verified stability in production.

### Deadlock Elimination: Resource Ordering vs. DAG Execution Ordering

The early multi-repo document conflated the order of lock acquisition with the order of code execution. These are two distinct operational requirements:

* **Deterministic Lock Ordering (Deadlock Avoidance):** If Transaction 1 touches `[sower, bible]` and Transaction 2 touches `[bible, sower]`, concurrent dispatches will deadlock. The coordinator enforces global **alphanumeric lock acquisition**:

$$\text{LockOrder} = \text{SortAlphabetical}(\text{target\_repos})$$



Every coordinator acquires repository mutexes in this exact sequence, mathematically eliminating circular-wait deadlocks.
* **DAG Execution Ordering (Causal Dependencies):** Once locks are secured, code dispatch follows the topological dependency graph:

$$\text{ExecutionOrder} = \text{TopologicalSort}(\text{DependencyDAG})$$



`goblin-config` builds first, emits packages to the local registry, `goblin-bible` consumes them, and `worker-sower-engine` compiles against the resulting state.

### The Parent Transaction Coordinator FSM (`MultiRepoTransaction.ts`)

```typescript
export type MultiRepoState =
  | 'INITIALIZING'
  | 'LOCKS_ACQUIRED'
  | 'CHILD_TASKS_DISPATCHED'
  | 'ALL_CHILDREN_VERIFIED'
  | 'MERGING_FORWARD'
  | 'PARTIALLY_MERGED'
  | 'COMPLETED'
  | 'COMPENSATING_REVERT'
  | 'ABORTED';

export interface MultiRepoTransactionContext {
  transactionId: string;
  targetRepos: string[]; // Alphanumerically sorted
  childTaskIds: Record<string, string>; // repo -> taskId
  mergeSequence: string[]; // Topologically sorted DAG order
  successfulMerges: string[];
  failedRepo?: string;
  errorReason?: string;
}

```

* **Handling Partial Merges Without History Rewrites:** If a failure occurs after Repository 1 merges but before Repository 2 merges, the coordinator transitions to `PARTIALLY_MERGED`. It is strictly forbidden from executing `git reset --hard` on `main`.
* Instead, the coordinator inspects its forward-compatibility contract:
* If the upstream merge was purely additive, it parks the transaction, halts downstream dispatches, and generates an automated advisory card in Slack `#ops-bridge`.
* If the change was breaking, the outbox dispatches an automated **Compensating Revert PR** against Repository 1, merging the revert cleanly through the standard pull-request gauntlet.
